headline: The Truth About The Ferguson Case That Most People Won't Acknowledge
lede:
Some things I have learned:

Pro Publica recently did an in-depth analysis and found that black kids between the ages of 15-19 are 21 times more likely to be shot and killed by cops than white kids of the same age. That's an insane statistic. That's per capita, not actual numbers. If you are a black teenage boy, you have a 21x higher risk of being shot by police.

Also, in 2010, Federal prosecutors took 162,000 cases to a grand jury. You know how many DIDN'T go to trial? 6.

Also, Mike Brown's family will never get a state criminal trial to get justice for their son. And the testimony that denied them that right technically doesn't make any sense. Seriously, go read it.

headline: While The Rest Of The World Wasn't Looking, Mongolia Managed To Achieve Something Kind Of Amazing
lede:
The Overseas Development Institute has released a new report on Mongolia that's amazing. Even though up to 40% of its population is nomadic, the country has found a way to achieve something wealthier nations can only envy: 98% of its girls and 93% of its boys are now getting a secondary education.

Mongolians value the education of their kids above almost everything else, and now their government — flush with money from a mining boom and improved taxation — has taken up the challenge of paying for it. With a completely overhauled modern education policy that's more responsive to families' needs, and with the support of external financing partners, they're actually getting it done.

excerpt: Investigative journalist Chai Jing's self-funded documentary, "Under The Dome," about the long term effects of air pollution in China went massively viral at the beginning of March 2015, racking up over 150 million views in it's first weekend alone.
headline: EXCLUSIVE: A massively viral Chinese documentary, summarized in English for the first time.
lede:
Retired investigative journalist Chai Jing's self-funded documentary, "Under The Dome," about the long term effects of air pollution in China went massively viral at the beginning of March 2015, racking up over 150 million views in it's first weekend alone.

We at Upworthy felt it was so important to share the documentary with non-Mandarin speakers that we commissioned exclusive translations of the first and last 10 minutes of the documentary, and embedded them below.

To fill in the middle, however, we called on Upworthy's Head of Product, Mike Su, who grew up in Taiwan and speaks fluent Mandarin to provide a play-by-play.
share_text: Over 150 million people have seen her film, but few English-speakers could understand it. Until now.

headline: Why Do Sexual Assault Survivors Feel Shame? A Cartoon Sums It Up. By The 4th Panel, I'm Taken Aback.
lede:
Trigger warning: Discussion of rape, sexual assault, abuse.

Almost every survivor of sexual assault or abuse will at one point think, "It was my fault." What many of us don't know is WHY survivors feel shame and guilt or why others around them might blame them instead of the perpetrator. The following cartoon breaks down the reasons why.

So, to all the survivors out there who are blaming themselves for what happened, here's the psychology behind why you might feel so guilty. I'm crossing my fingers that at least a couple of you will read this and finally feel some solace.

And for anyone who has ever asked, "Why didn't she run away?" or "Why didn't he scream?" This one's for you, too.

headline: This Filmmaker’s Showing Hollywood What A Real Leading Lady Looks Like. Glad We + You Could Help.
lede:
Iyin Landre is a super inspiring woman who realized that 1) Hollywood wasn't going to look past the fact that she (like many Americans) is not white and 2) the only way she'd be able to play a non-stereotypical character in a film was if she made the movie herself. So she made a Kickstarter video to fund her movie, Me + You.

Upworthy curator Carolyn Silveira found and shared the video, and in less than two days helped secure 80% of the funding Iyin needed to make the film. The Kickstarter reached its goal, and Iyin's now in Brazil tightening up the script and hiring a dream team.

We couldn't resist sharing the very sweet video she sent to Carolyn with all of you...

headline: A Straight Reporter Says "I'd Be Offended By You If I Were Gay." This Actor's Response? Epic.
lede:
As a gay who dates online, I often come across the term "straight-acting" in reference to what the guy I'm looking at wants in a partner, or how he acts himself. What that term implies, to me at least, is "acceptable to be seen with". In my opinion, that's pretty twisted thinking.

Jordan Gavaris plays fellow shiny shoe owner Felix Dawkins in "Orphan Black", one of the more "stereotypically gay" characters on TV today. I can only imagine Jordan gets asked this question about Felix all the time, but what a great answer he gives.

headline: Here’s Pete Seeger Doing One Of The Songs He Loved So Much
lede:
I saw Pete Seeger in Seattle about 15 years ago, with Ani DiFranco and several other musicians; they did a version of “We Shall Overcome” that absolutely stunned the entire concert hall, with everybody holding hands and singing along in one of those powerful and electric moments that can happen when humans connect over music.

This clip is from the 2009 inauguration ceremony of newly-elected President Obama. Pete Seeger came to play a little music with Bruce Springsteen, Seeger’s grandson Tao, and many others. Originally written by Woody Guthrie, who Seeger performed with many times, it’s a powerful version of “This Land Is Your Land,” with lyrics (including the frequently-forgotten last few stanzas!) below the video. As always, Pete tried to get the crowd to sing along, shouting out the lyrics so they could all join in.

We’ll miss you, Pete.

headline: WARNING: This Type Of Dancing Can Lead To Severe Empowerment And A Strong Connection With Others
lede:
Valentine's Day is usually reserved for chocolates and those (really gross) candy hearts that say things like, "Call Me." (Seriously though. Are they just straight up made of chalk?) However, the past couple of years have been a little different. Eve Ensler, who penned "The Vagina Monologues," has started a movement to end violence against women. And when I say "movement," I really mean movement! People all over the world are getting together to dance and demand justice for survivors of violence.

The moves are really easy, I swear. The song is called, "Break the Chain," and the instructions are underneath the video. This video shows some of last year's gatherings, and they are spectacular.

Forget the cheesy greeting cards. Let's spread a message that really matters.

headline: A Company Ignores Hateful Response, Proceeds With Regular Advertising Aimed At Regular Families
lede:
A while ago, Cheerios aired a regular commercial, featuring regular parents and a regular (although very cute) little girl. But wow, did that ordinary ad bring out the ugly in a lot of people. Cheerios had to disable the comments to put a stop to the racist hate that was being directed toward the fictional interracial family. How is this even a thing any more?

Clearly, the company isn't being deterred by the haters because this cute sequel, where the little girl learns things are about to change, is going to air during the Super Bowl. I love it when a company chooses to ignore a very loud, but very wrong group.

lede:

lede:

lede:

And if your refresher course comes from 25+ brilliant minds who work hard to uphold our human rights? Bonus.

I especially appreciate what they say starting at 2:40 - just who are the people we need protecting from? And at 3:06 I feel encouraged to keep speaking up on social media platforms (I hope you do, too). At 4:12, a quick, eye-opening story about how it feels to be denied your human rights is all the reminder we should need to keep working on these issues.

lede:

headline: It's Been Over 100 Years Since An Artist Has Done This In America. About Time Someone Did It Again.
lede:
More than a century has passed since a photographic journey explored Native Americans with such a broad scope and in this amount of detail. In 1906 photographer Edward S. Curtis was commissioned by J.P. Morgan to capture the “disappearing” race.

In 2014, to change perceptions about American Indians, photographer Matika Wilbur believes have to update the kind of imagery we're looking at when we think of her race. It's a beautiful — and important — idea.

headline: Welcome To Solitary Confinement U.S. Style
lede:
In 2009 three Americans were hiking near the Iran-Iraq border when they were captured and imprisoned. They were accused of being spies and kept in an Iranian prison without a trial for two years. (One hiker was released after a little over a year.) In this video, one of the hikers, Shane Bauer, tours an American prison's solitary unit to see how it compares to where he stayed in isolation in Iran for four long months.

Warning: A NSFW moment happens at around 2:42.

headline: Pussy Riot's Witty Reply To Stephen Colbert's Question: "Will They Stop Being Gay?'
lede:
Pussy Riot were famed as the punk band in Russia who were imprisoned after they spoke out, and protested against, their government for their brutal repression of freedom.

So when two of the Pussy Riot members* Maria Alyokhina and Nadezhda Tolokonnikova were eventually released, they made an appearance on The Colbert Show to speak out against the human rights violations in their home country. From it, I just had to highlight the hilarious response they gave to Stephen's satirical question about gay people in Russia.

headline: See The Forest That's Growing Within A Concrete Block In Milan
lede:
What's that over there? Is that two large building blocks in the middle of Milan covered in a rich, green forest? Why yes, yes it is.

In the Porta Nuova district of Milan, Italy there is a pair of residential towers that (will) host more than 900 trees on 8,900 square metres of terraces as part of a 'rehabilitation' of the historic district. Or in other terms: lots and lots of trees in a tiny, little space to make the place look prettier. An ace, creative idea.

Oh and just a side thought about the video: how much does the man at 0:23 in look like Hugh Jackman?! IS HE HUGH JACKMAN'S LONG LOST TWIN BROTHER.

headline: Breaking The Mold Like This Football Player Just Did Isn't Easy, But It's Certainly Wonderful
lede:
Michael Sam is a defensive lineman for the University of Missouri's Mizzou Tigers. He opened up about his personal life by coming out, potentially becoming the first openly gay NFL player in history.

Being gay in (or on) any field shouldn't matter at all, but since Sam may be a first in his sport to live openly, it really really matters. The only way out of a culture of silence is through.

headline: Don't Look Now, But Our Country Is In A Place It Hasn't Been For Well Over 100 Years
lede:
A few definitions to tee this up:

Oligarchy: A society where power is in the hands of very few people, usually determined by wealth, corporate and family ties, and the military.

The Gilded Age: From the 1870s to the 1900s, our country was run by very few people (think John D. Rockefeller, J.P. Morgan, Andrew W. Mellon, Andrew Carnegie) but also marked by extreme poverty. The term was coined by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner to mean, "an era of serious social problems disguised by thin gold gilding."

So ... are we there yet?!

headline: When A Black Actor Can't 'Act Black', What'll He Do? Whatever You're Thinking, You're Not Prepared.
lede:
I used to be in plays in high school. As all adolescent theater dorks do, between rehearsals and harmonising to Top 40 songs in the car, I considered going into acting. I ended up deciding against it mostly because I thought I was really terrible acting the way I saw most black actors acting in television and movies in the late '90s.

Still, minority actors are faced with that dilemma all the time: should they refuse to become a stereotype, or should they actually get to work?

headline: This Man Was Jailed For Him Beliefs, But Now He's Found A Way To Tell His Story
lede:
Burma has a long riddled history of repression, and even though we've seen the country taking progressive steps towards freedom in recent years, a lot of people are like "Er, keep your eyes open world, this is just cosmetic change — there's still a ton of political prisoners, in-discriminative killings of ethnic groups, and no freedom to say out loud that the government is total shit."

This man below was imprisoned for his beliefs and for taking part in peaceful demonstrations. When he was released, there were so many barriers in place for him to live a normal life. Fortunately he and some other former political prisoners found this smart way of making an income *and* keep their story alive.

headline: Sometimes The Daily Show Isn't As Much Funny As It Is Really Powerful And Beautiful
lede: In the run up to the Sochi Olympics, there was uproar over Russia's awful anti-gay laws that were destroying lives and families. The Daily Show decided to head over to find out what the deal was and interviewed one of Putin's spokesmen. Said spokesman confirmed all their worst fears. So Jason Jones went onto the streets to find out more. And although he discovered 74% of Russians are anti-gay, he also found pockets of beautiful dissent. At 4:06, he asks the people that really matter, a bunch of LGBTQ Russians, why they don't just leave. At 5:40, he meets an amazing woman who actually makes me tear up a little. It doesn't even end with a joke.

headline: If Classic Movies Were Recast With Black People, Would They Still Be Classic?
lede:
I think the fact that this looks so new and unfamiliar (even to someone like me) brings up something to think about: Hollywood casting is ... well ... not so colorful.

Think, if Audrey Hepburn were black, would she have been in "Breakfast at Tiffany's"? If you're saying to yourself, "Surely her talent would have made her a success," think about how many classic movies Lena Horne or Dorothy Dandridge were in. And if Jada Pinkett-Smith's character in "The Matrix" was the lead (and not a supporting character), would we have cared about the movie as much? When stuff like this is the norm: ask yourself why we can't we have movie classics with leading black women where she doesn't play a slave or a maid?

These absolutely gorgeous images by Senegalese photographer Omar Victor Diop and French-American photographer Antoine Tempé have got me thinking as I get lost in the beauty.

headline: A Gorgeous Model Worked The Runway At Fashion Week. You May Notice Something Different About Her.
lede:
In an ideal world, the people who model clothes will be relatable to us. Fashion designer Carrie Hammer made her debut at New York Fashion week by hitting it out of the park. She chose to feature Danielle Sheypuk, someone Hammer calls a "role model," in her runway show.

I was presented with the question: "Did you even notice the dress?" And to be honest, it took me a while because I was so thrilled to see someone who doesn't fit the traditional runway model mold. Hopefully this is the first step. Maybe seeing models with different body types and disabilities will become common enough that the first thing we notice is what they're wearing. Isn't that the purpose of a runway show?

Yay for smart ideas that address the serious imbalance of wealth!

Watch these Walking Dead, Harry Potter, and film stars act as country leaders and take a look at what the world might be like in 2024 with this tax in place and adopted by a bunch of countries... except my country, England.

headline: They Worked On It For 9 Long Years. Now's Your Chance To See It In Person.
lede:
A few months ago, we posted about a fundraiser for the Beehive Design Collective. What's the Beehive Design Collective, you ask? It's a group of amazing artists that creates story graphics on themes of globalization and resistance. Their work is fantastically detailed and chock-full of both history and passion.

The Bees' most recent poster (the subject of their fundraising campaign) is called Mesoamérica Resiste. It tells stories of resistance, resilience, and solidarity from Mexico to Colombia. It shows the modern invasion of megaprojects planned for the region as well as grassroots efforts to defend land and traditions, protect cultural and ecological diversity, and build alternative economies.

So whatever happened with that campaign? Well, in large part thanks to Upworthians like you donating and sharing the post, the Bees more than tripled their fundraising and outreach goals, ending up just a few dollars short of a whopping $118,000 from 3,000 backers around the world.

But the story's not over! You can learn about the next chapter of the Bee's adventure once the poster went to print and watch the video below.

lede:
Okay, let's give college bulletins and the glossy magazines the benefit of the doubt: maybe they're seriously concerned with stopping rapes on campuses (and elsewhere). And maybe they sincerely believe that a good way to do that is to suggest some of the steps you'll see below.

Namely, rapists. I'd much rather see a discussion about how we get men to understand consent and stop being creepers than the bizarre, contradictory wardrobe suggestions brilliantly parodied in this video.

headline: Here Are Some Posters For The Men Who Tell Women What To Do Or What They Think Of Them In The Street
lede:
Every day women are harassed in the street simply by being a woman. Or in other words: every time we step out the house we run the risk of being shouted at, cat-called or assaulted usually in broad daylight. FUN!

Brooklyn based artist Tatyana Fazlalizadeh wanted to take women's voices and faces and plaster them big and bold in the very same places where this takes place. She's addressing gender based street harassment by taking a place where women feel uncomfortable and turning it into a place where we cannot be ignored through street art, and that is pretty awesome.

lede:

We thought it would be pretty cool if toy makers took notice and started creating dolls for our kids that are more realistic.

Well, that hasn't happened, so Nickolay decided to make his own "average" dolls. He's running a crowdfunding project, and you can help support it by donating or ordering a doll.

headline: Have Our Beauty Standards Gotten So Bad That They Affect Even Our Fruits And Vegetables?
lede:
A few students in Germany have started advocating for ugly fruits and vegetables. Everyone needs their own advocacy group, right? Even strawberries! OK, so really what they're advocating for is less food waste. Tons of food is discarded every day around the world because it doesn't match the aesthetics of what someone decided fruits and veggies were supposed to look like. Who decides these things, anyway?

Long story short (too late, I know): If we were allowed to purchase the "ugly" fruits and vegetables, we could eliminate a bucketload of unnecessary waste.

headline: Have You Seen Banksy's New Artwork That Stands With Syria?
lede:
The Syria crisis hasn't slowed down, and over 100,000 people have died in three years, with thousands of mostly women and children displaced.

But people are standing with Syria, including the street artist Banksy who has re-worked his famous and popular art work of a girl reaching for a red balloon with the intention of shedding light on the Syrian crisis. The original artwork depicted a young girl with flowing hair, with a heart shaped balloon just beyond her grasp — the new re-working of his classic stencil is of a young Syrian girl accompanied with a #WithSyria hashtag.

See the creative way Banksy is using his famous platform to draw attention to the ongoing crisis in the image below.

headline: Some Helpful, Smart Advice On What To Do If Someone Close Tells You They've Been Raped
lede:
It's a horrifying and stark reality that rape is a crime that seeps into all corners of society: it affects men, women, people from privileged backgrounds, people from poorer backgrounds, young and old. It is a crime used as a tool of power, and more often than it is an issue that many people attempt to push aside, belittle or pretend doesn't exist.

But for the people who are affected by the crime, it is never something that just disappears. Every person copes in different ways, and below are some good guidelines to keep in mind if anyone you care about confides in you that they've experienced something extremely traumatizing. The tips are from a 21 year old survivor who detailed some helpful advice on his 'Self-Care after Rape' blog.

headline: There's More To Life Than Being Really, Really, Ridiculously Good Looking
lede:
We all have those days where you feel kinda rough-gross-want-to-curl-up-and-hide-ugly. But you know the best thing to do? Stop looking at model selfies on Instagram, avoid scrolling through websites full of photos of celebrities in bikinis, stop hating yourself for not going to the gym today, and just listen to these classic jams below.

Honestly, if TLC's "Unpretty", India Arie's "Video", Christina Aguilera's "Beautiful" and Destiny's Child's "Bootylicious" can't make your life immeasurably better, I don't know what will. And hey, some will think that this is a trivial way to address body image issues, but these songs became my personal anthems and shaped how I felt about myself growing up, so I'm hoping they make you feel a little less "ugh" and a little more "hey my face is nice."

And yes, that headline is a reference to the film Zoolander.

2. Who is Rupert and why did he have a land in present-day North Dakota until the early 1800's?

3. Maybe all this crowing about the securing our borders is missing about 200 years of rich context with regard to just how flexible these borders have been.

What caught your eye about this map, Internet? Or am I just nerding out by myself over here?

headline: There Are So Many Great Books Here, And Yet So Many You Won’t Read In School
lede:
I think it’s really weird that in school you always have to read books that are decades if not centuries old. Don’t get me wrong, they’re great books and they should be read. But it irks me that there’s a derisive attitude towards books written more recently (what, we can't teach "Harry Potter" or "Eleanor & Park" in school?) and I can’t quite figure out why. Is it because they’re written in more modern language that's easier to understand? Is it because kids might actually enjoy them, and heaven forbid we make learning fun and accessible? What is it?

Here’s a list of fantastic books written in the 21st century. It’s a great example of how many wonderful books have been written in our recent past, and I think more of them should be taught in schools. Except for "Twilight." Burn the "Twilight" books.

So there's this site called Quora.com. A lot of people write there, myself included. A few of the writers there got together and decided to help a fellow Quoran and ranger in Zambia, Rory Young, in his efforts to prevent the extinction of African Elephants. They could become extinct within 6 years if action isn't taken. So learn more about what they're doing, and if you are up for it, spread the word and help.

headline: Creative People Are An Endangered Species. Are You On The Chopping Block?
lede: A curious phenomenon has crept into the school systems all across the world, and it's threatening to violently derail social progress. Sir Ken Robinson brilliantly describes the death of creativity in the name of education with perhaps the driest British wit in existence. From the idea that literally everyone he knows has a serious interest in education at 1:13, to the globally recognized hierarchy of school subjects at 8:47, to the way teachers literally steer future artists and poets away from their desired fields at 11:32, Sir Robinson paints a bleak, although avoidable picture of the probable future. He also drops a truth bomb about the depreciated value of education at 12:40, and relays a wonderful case study from a woman whose artistic work you've almost certainly seen before at 15:22. Stay tuned until 18:23 for a hopeful conclusion.

lede: The United States has a massive problem in the form of a runaway prison system. Since you've had your ears open at some point in the past five years, you'll know that prisons fuel their own vicious cycles of prisoner aggregation and retention. If we don't do something, it's going to continue to get worse. Education reform within prisons would dramatically reduce prisoner relapse, the prison population as a whole, and the the prison system's cost to taxpayers. I mean this in every way: We'd be stupid not to do it.

lede:
Derek Paravicini is a magnificent pianist. He also happens to be blind and autistic. Here we get a peek at how his beautiful brain helps his fingers make beautiful music.

The video starts with some background on Derek’s life. At 7:45, Derek’s teacher takes us inside the mind of the musical genius. Tune in at 9:56 to hear a piece you’ll definitely recognize (and one Derek was playing impeccably at 11). And stick around at 11:55 to hear the same song — miraculously — in two other keys. Then, at 13:22, he takes audience requests. Finally, at 16:10, we hear Derek’s rendition of “Chopsticks” and learn why he’s not just a “human iPod,” but a brilliant musician.

lede:
Big news: the Supreme Court seem think that a law to stop southern states making it hard for people of color to vote, The Voting Rights Act, has "served its purpose" and "does not reflect racial progress" in America, and today they struck down a crucial part of it. Come on guys, DUH! Racism is soooo over! Obama is black!
Luckily for us living in the non-magical-bubble-of-ignorance land, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg explains below why the law is still crucial today, and gives an example as to why we still need it for the sake of civil rights in modern America.

headline: What's The Dumbest Thing You Could Say To A Congresswoman Who Lost Her Legs In Battle? FOUND IT.
lede: An IRS contractor under investigation was using his injured veteran status to get $500 Million contracts. Problem is, he never served. He went to a military school and hurt his foot playing football. He kept playing through his injury. Then one day, decades later, he used it to get preferred treatment in military contracts. Rep. Tammy Duckworth who lost both her legs and still could lose her arm from combat injuries felt that this might just be a touch inappropriate. Especially after he wrote a letter to the Veterans Administration that read in part, "These are crosses that I bear due to my service to our great country and I would do it again to protect this great country." So she gave him the interrogation he deserved. It gets amazing at around 4:30.

headline: Sorry, We Broke You, And There’s No Legal Way To Put You Back Together
lede:
I can't imagine being taken away from my home and family and told I can never return. Can you? But that's what we’re doing: ripping families apart. And then making it so that they can't legally be put back together. These are real people — and there are thousands more like them — whose lives have been turned upside down by our inability to figure out this issue.

Are there really people who still argue that our system isn’t broken? How many more of these stories have to be told before we see real change?

headline: Malala Was Shot By The Taliban – And It Made Her Father Encourage Her To Speak Out Even More
lede:
Ziauddin Yousafzai’s daughter Malala was shot by the Taliban in 2012 after she has just boarded a bus to school. Today, Malala is now recognised around the world as a global leader for women's rights ... at the age of 16.

Ziauddin explains in his TED talk how he was determined to raise his daughter to be strong, confident, and passionate. He stresses that the plight of millions of women could be changed if both men and women think differently and break against the norms of family and society.

His message gives an inspiring lesson for all of us — fathers, mothers, men, women — to hear.

The Bechdel Test was created by Allison Bechdel and it is just a simple way of evaluating if women talk about anything other than men — jobs, friendships, politics, life... seriously, anything else.

Perhaps it's time for us to make up our own word right here in the good ol' U.S. of A. for being worked to death. 

These charts show the 20 other "rich" countries that beat us out on mandated paid holidays and paid vacation time. No wonder folks are a little tense on the job...

headline: I'm Not Sure I Could Do What This Actress Did—In Front Of A Police Car—In A Foreign Country...
lede: What actress Tilda Swinton did in Russia is courage defined. Below she's holding a pride flag in Red Square. That seems like no big deal until you know that it's illegal in Russia to have "propaganda of nontraditional sexual relations" in public places. That basically means you can't show any support for LGBTQIA causes at all. You can be imprisoned for even holding a rainbow flag like Swinton is doing here — right in front of the Russian police.

lede:

At 0.50, someone actually takes candy from babies. No, really. At 3:00, we start to see the science unfold before our eyes. Entire management courses could — and should — be taught with the bit starting at 04:40.

headline: Its Not A Hymn For Hoodies. Its Vintage Crackling Commentary On Trayvon, Set To Music.
lede:
Before things got cloudy in the killing of Trayvon Martin trial, we have to go back to that window of time between his death and when there had not even been an arrest made. Why had that taken so long? What was the delay? Thats what I remember asking. The reasons for that oh-too-long pause, exemplified through this song, gives us a peaceful reminder of how hard it was to get justice in motion and now, how much further justice has to go.

The line that really gets to me comes at 3:25 because it calls attention to such a simple fact, and yet it became so much more than that.

headline: I Don’t Think Eminem Realizes He’s Become A Science Teacher
lede:
Nas, Tupac, Common, Public Enemy … these rappers taught this white British girl living in a small village about the ways of world. No really, I learnt (and sang along to) every word to Lauryn Hill's Miseducation album at the age of 13. I still do.

Embarrassing confessions aside, this is why I was so happy to see this incredibly innovative teaching method: combine something you love (rap) with something valuable (education) and look at how the kids faces light up with joy when they realize that real learning isn't just text books, whiteboards and tests.

headline: See How One Couple In Los Angeles Squeezes An Entire Farm Into A Small City Home
lede:
Erik and Kelly decided they'd rather grow their own artichokes than have to work at crummy jobs in order to buy them at the store. So naturally, they turned their urban house into a mini-farm.

I loved this home tour because it's also a radical reminder of what "home economics" really means. Learn why they actually hate the idea of "self-sufficiency" at 2:00, hear about a time when everyone in L.A. had chickens at 6:00, and check out their exotic milk-crate toilet at 11:00.

headline: Is This The Most Real Talk You'll Ever See In A Tampon Commercial?
lede: FINALLY! An ad that normalizes talking about periods for a younger crowd. Getting your period is SO not something to be embarrassed about, but you'd never guess that from the way most tampon and pad ads go out of their way to not talk about what their products are used for. I'm really glad this ad doesn't try to cover up what a period is with poetic language, nondescript neon-blue liquid demonstrations, or slow-mo shots of girls dancing on beaches in white pants. Periods are normal. Talking about them and how to handle them should be normal, too.

headline: You Might Recall The Old Song, 'This Land Is Your Land' But Did You Know Why It's Kinda Subversive?
lede:
The last part of the old Woody Guthrie favorite, "This Land Is Your Land," is usually left off of printed versions of the song, because some deemed it a bit too ... edgy for schoolkids. To me, the lyrics are quite wonderful, and spot-on for our hard times:

In the shadow of the steeple I saw my people,
By the relief office I seen my people;
As they stood there hungry, I stood there asking
Is this land made for you and me?

headline: Photographer Introduces Us To The Army's Version Of The Chastity Belt.
lede:
Photographer and Air Force veteran Stacy Pearsall captures Army basic trainees in all their glory. For this set, she profiles only the Soldiers who wear BCGs, affectionately known as Birth Control Glasses. I want to show you these pics to squash any misconceived notion that the military is only filled with G.I. Joe or Jane’s with six-packs and mohawks. This is the basic training I remember. Young, too young, kids who raise their right hand for whatever reason. Ask our decision makers to remember that whenever you feel they're asking too much from our stretched military.

All photos provided by Stacy L. Pearsall.

headline: Hands Down, The Quickest Way To Kick Start The Economy Is To Do Something Very Simple
lede: There's no doubt about it: raising the minimum wage isn't just a matter of economic justice, it's also a women's equality issue. Especially since close to 60% of minimum wage earners are women, many of them with children. And guess what? If we raised the minimum wage, it would move many of them off of SNAP and other social services. Win/win, right?

On New York City’s Governers Island stands a structure large enough to dance in and filled with bright beautiful light during the day. The good people of Studio KCA created their “Head in the Clouds” pavilion out of 53,780 plastic bottle and jugs- the number of plastic bottles thrown away in New York City in just 1 hour. The whole idea behind this pillowy beauty was to call attention to the nearly 48,000,000 plastic bottles thrown away every day in the United States.

lede:

This is calculating how much it might cost, and how much money the government will chip in, for people who choose to buy the new health insurance plans available in the "exchange," or "Marketplace," starting in 2014.

headline: Congress Did Something So Spectacularly Creepy That It's Too Unbelievable To Make Up
lede:
On the House floor, Congressman Chris Van Hollen decided to get a clarification on the rules of the shutdown. Apparently, normally, any congressperson can call for a vote on any bill at any time. But just before the shutdown happened, the GOP quietly passed a measure that said only the House Majority Leader, Eric Cantor, can call for the shutdown to end. Not even the most senior GOP congressperson, Speaker of the House John Boehner, is allowed to do it.

Here's the thing. Democrats are not always right. Neither are Republicans. The political system is messed up from top to bottom. But this is just crazy. The guy in charge of the GOP can't end the shutdown. Watch and see. At 5:00, we get to the reality of the situation.

headline: We've Gotten Used To Hearing About This Kind Of Violence, But Let's Not Forget The Impact Of It
lede: I worry that "bullying" has become one of those words that we hear so often, we sometimes don't consider the gravity of it. I know I hear and read it over and over each day. But the thing is, bullying is such a problem that we have to keep talking about it. And we need to continue working to stop it. As a parent, it's a regular topic of conversation in our home. Equally important, my husband and I try our best to model the kind of behavior we want our kids to emulate. I don't have the answers, but I do know that when 3 million kids skip school each month because they feel unsafe, we have a lot of work to do. These statistics are jarring.

headline: Watch Statistics Transform Into People You Know And Understand, Right Before Your Very Eyes
lede:
The statistics about Syria's refugees right now, if you dare to look at them, are scary: millions of people fleeing one country and arriving in dire need of help in other countries. Half are children.

But if you look at this portrait project, the numbers fall away and there is a familiar story: people who love their families, friends, country, and lives, and who just want to return to them.

What is a "refugee"? A person who misses home.

headline: We've Gotten Used To Hearing About This Kind Of Violence, But Let's Not Forget The Impact Of It
lede: I worry that "bullying" has become one of those words that we hear so often, we sometimes don't consider the gravity of it. I know I hear and read it over and over each day. But the thing is, bullying is such a problem that we have to keep talking about it. And we need to continue working to stop it. As a parent, it's a regular topic of conversation in our home. Equally important, my husband and I try our best to model the kind of behavior we want our kids to emulate. I don't have the answers, but I do know that when 3 million kids skip school each month because they feel unsafe, we have a lot of work to do. These statistics are jarring.

headline: Watch Kerry Washington Play Every Black Woman Alive Right Now On SNL
lede:
In case you missed it, Saturday Night Live has come under fire for not having a black woman on its cast since Maya Rudolph left in 2007. In fact, they've only had three — out of the 137 cast members they've cast since the start of the show. To make matters worse, Kenan Thompson said "It's just a tough part of the business ... like in auditions, they just never find ones that are ready." I guess they haven't been able to find any since the show started in 1975...

I thought the point of a sketch comedy show is to have actors that can represent the world we live in so there's not a Shakespeare-Globe-Theater-every-lady-is-played-by-a-dude situation. Apparently SNL doesn't agree.

headline: This Rap Song Is About Girls And Money But Not In That Way
lede:

Ruby Bridges was the first African American to attend an all white elementary school in 1960 in New Orleans. She made history that day — but all she knew was that she starting a new day of school and that she should make some new friends.

lede:

Beneath his honest and heartbreaking account is a call for drastic action to be taken. Isn't it time?

headline: Another Guy In A Suit Talking About Our School System. Except This One's A Student. And He Nails It.
lede:
Common Core standards were created to equalize education across income lines. The purpose was to make available to students from poor families the quality of education available to students from more affluent families.

However, the extreme focus on testing might just be creating an education system that lacks a whole lot of things that are really, really important. This kid nails the problem with Common Core in a way I've not yet heard, claiming that we're ruining the way we teach and learn. It's keeping teachers from doing what they're so good at and students from being real human learners.

Just listen to what he has to say. If he gets it as a student, it's hard for me to understand how the adults who are implementing it don't see the problem.

headline: Feeling Crappy? Hear This Little Song Remind You That Things May Not Be Too Bad
lede:
You may have a lot of baggage in your life right now, and it's okay to complain about it. But this fun little song by the amazing Tim Minchin is a nice little reminder that we sometimes forget that most of us probably have it pretty good.

Don't get me wrong, I don't mean you should watch this and think "thankfully my life isn't THAT screwed compared to {insert person/group of people living through hardship} ammmmmirite?!", but it's just a gentle nudge to sometimes stop talking, reflect, think of the good things you do have, and smile. If that fails, Google some photos of cute puppies.

What kind of backward sense does that make?

Giving Tuesday is the solution to the inevitable guilt you'll have after all your Cyber Monday clicking finger nets you a deal on that iPad you've been craving all year.

What kind of backward sense does that make?

Giving Tuesday is the solution to the inevitable guilt you'll have after all your Cyber Monday clicking finger nets you a deal on that iPad you've been craving all year.

headline: We Don’t Hear Enough From Native American Voices. Here’s An Inspiring Message From One.
lede:
The Oglala Lakota live on Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota, near the Black Hills. The area has a pretty tragic history of violence, broken treaties, and culture clashes, beginning in 1874, when prospectors discovered gold in the Black Hills and the the U.S. government seized the land that had previously been guaranteed to the tribe.

Today, what little we hear about the reservation is usually about the poverty, violence, and alcoholism. While that does exist, that is just one story of many. I wish we heard more stories like this, about the beauty of the land and the spirituality and strength of the people.

headline: One Amazing TEDx Talk + 8 Million Views = One Life Changing Moment
lede:
At the beginning of November 2013, one of Upworthy’s curators shared a fantastic TEDx talk by a woman named Ash Beckham about having difficult conversations. According to Ash, the video had been out for about a month and had around 2,000 views when Upworthy got ahold of it. It now has over 8 million.

One of those views was by a kid who came up to Ash after a presentation and told her something incredibly moving. Ash was kind enough to share her story with us, and we wanted to share it with you because we think it’s pretty amazing that something as simple as sharing a video can change a life. Be prepared to get out the Kleenex around 4:00.

headline: Sometimes, Silence Is A Good Thing. Here, It's Most Definitely Not.
lede:
I want to be really clear: I'm not anti-gun. I grew up around guns and I'm still very comfortable handling them. I know many people feel differently and that's okay.

But the point I hope we can all agree on is that something has to change. 35,000 people should not die from gun violence every year. Parents shouldn't ever have to worry that their kids might be shot at school.

We should absolutely observe a moment of silence for terrible tragedies, but we need to remember as part of the bigger picture that silence won't result in change. A majority of Americans, including NRA members, agree that background checks are important. So let's start with universal background checks for private gun sales.

excerpt: He died too young. So all his friends got together to make sure future generations don't.
headline: A Kid Looked Death Right In The Eye And Sang This Song. 5000 People Picked Up Where He Left Off.
lede:
Back in May of 2013, my life was changed forever. A fan had written me to let me know that a teenage musician named Zach Sobiech that I had written about earlier in the year had just passed away from a rare cancer. Zach had written a song about coming to terms his imminent death called "Clouds." Cancer is personal to me, you see, as I've lost many people, including my father to it. My mom has hers under control. My son will inevitably have to do something to make sure he doesn't get it. It hit too close to home.

The day Zach passed, I went online to see if I could find any more videos about him to honor his memory, and discovered an amazing documentary short about his brief but beautiful life. I spent a whole day crying, having flashbacks to my father's passing, and made sure it could reach as many people as possible. It was the biggest hit we ever had. 20,000,000 people have seen it. People emailed me from all over the globe to talk about how his story impacted their lives. Parents tweeted me about their lost children. Upworthy readers helped raise $450,000 for the Children's Cancer Fund. His song went on to become the 1st independent artist to reach the top of the iTunes music charts. And I got to know a wonderful team of people who actually knew and loved him.

I'm sad I never got the opportunity to meet him. But 5000 people who did really know him got together to create a giant choir in the middle of Mall of America. lede:

The excuse? A psychologist (being questioned by Anderson below) said he suffered from affluenza: being a rich kid and thus, as a young person of wealth, having no consequences in life and not realising the severity of your actions.

Sure, psychologists the world over have said sentencing in this case is not atypical, but the reasoning behind it is something that we as a people need to put up for examination. The whole situation is pretty absurd.

headline: She Can Defend Herself — But Still, Why Don't Other People Speak Up When He Calls Her A Terrorist?
lede:
There are plenty of these type of 'What Would You Do?' videos online - where a fictional scenario of some sort of moral dilemma is played out in public and bystanders are filmed to see if they'd speak out. But while I was watching this, it struck me that this one was very different: instead of provoking a lot of responses like they usually do, the silence in this scenario one is deafening. Two people spoke out in two hours.

I can hear the 'but why do we think human compassion needs to be forced from bystanders?' criticism now of thse types of experiments — but what this experiment does do is offer a small insight into the public perception and the lack of education about why women chose to wear hijab, and as the YouTube creator Yousef Eraka says himself, "Yes, the women in hijab can defend themselves, but it doesn't hurt to know that her brothers and sisters in this country and other countries are by her side."

One year after Nirbhaya, a young girl in Delhi, was brutally raped on a bus, this Mumbai film school released a video highlighting the harrassment and unwanted attention women face while just trying to go about their day. It's meant to start a conversation about what empowerment for women looks like - this problem isn't unique to India, but it's definitely a place to start the conversation.

"Be a man" is something we've all heard at one time or another, even a few of the women reading this right now. Being a "man" in that sense means something completely different to me (and maybe you, too) than what that phrase implies.

I can't even begin to describe the toll that the concept of masculinity has taken on my life. And it's felt everywhere. It's time we make changes, starting from within ourselves.

headline: Feeling Anxious About Weed Legalization? Take A Hit Of This.
lede:
Marijuana is currently legal for recreational use in the great state of Colorado. In a few months, the same will be true of Washington state, as well. These facts have prompted pearl-clutching pieces from some prominent columnists about the effects they feel legalization will have on rates of marijuana usage and addiction as well as the more abstract threat they fear it poses to the moral fiber of American citizens.

Through magical feats of willful ignorance, these columns all somehow manage to sidestep the most important context surrounding the movement to legalize marijuana—which Chris Hayes helpfully provides in the form of an illustrative personal story.

headline: Do You Think That These Humans Were Created Equal After Seeing These Photos?
lede:
Humans, we're a funny bunch. We're quick to and pit people against each other in tribes: Liberal vs Conservative, Poor vs Rich, Old vs Young. But we seem to often overlook the fact that despite these seemingly obvious differences, we all still have the fundamental sameness.

That's what fascinated photographer Mark Laita, who decided to stand people of different backgrounds, occupations and appearances next to each other to, in his words, "let the viewer think for themselves about how the two individuals in the photographs relate and what that means."

headline: If Any Animal Is Going To Handle My Funeral, It Had Better Be An Elephant
lede:
Elephants are the only mammal aside from humans to have something approximating a funeral when their family member dies. They try to heal them, they comfort them, then they often have a rudimentary burial. Which brings me to the important part.

So there's this site called Quora.com. A lot of people write there, myself included. A few of the writers there got together and decided to help a fellow Quoran and ranger in Zambia, Rory Young, in his efforts to prevent the extinction of African Elephants. They could become extinct within 6 years if action isn't taken. So learn more about what they're doing, and if you are up for it, spread the word and help.

headline: What A Drone Targeting A Young Boy Cycling Would Look Like
lede:
The justification of drone strikes is that they target suspected terrorists — but what is so often left from the picture painted by politicians is the innocent lives that are taken.

Artist Omer Fast spoke with a former US drone operator in Afghanistan and Pakistan about the pilotless aircrafts — but instead of just filming the interview, he decided to show his words alongside a camera tracking a young boy cycling as if he were the target of a drone strike. It is a powerful and harrowing way to bring the issue closer to home and to close the empathy gap that exists when a problem seemingly only exists "far away."

headline: Some Helpful, Smart Advice On What To Do If Someone Close Tells You They've Been Raped
lede:
It's a horrifying and stark reality that rape is a crime that seeps into all corners of society: it affects men, women, people from privileged backgrounds, people from poorer backgrounds, young and old. It is a crime used as a tool of power, and more often than it is an issue that many people attempt to push aside, belittle or pretend doesn't exist.

But for the people who are affected by the crime, it is never something that just disappears. Every person copes in different ways, and below are some good guidelines to keep in mind if anyone you care about confides in you that they've experienced something extremely traumatizing. The tips are from a 21 year old survivor who detailed some helpful advice on his 'Self-Care after Rape' blog.

headline: Banksy Has Updated His Famous 'The Girl With The Balloon' Artwork To Stand With Syria
lede:
The Syria crisis hasn't slowed down, and over 100,000 people have died in three years, with thousands of mostly women and children displaced.

But people are standing with Syria, including the street artist Banksy who has re-worked his famous and popular art work of a girl reaching for a red balloon with the intention of shedding light on the Syrian crisis. The original artwork depicted a young girl with flowing hair, with a heart shaped balloon just beyond her grasp — the new re-working of his classic stencil is of a young Syrian girl accompanied with a #WithSyria hashtag.

See the creative way Banksy is using his famous platform to draw attention to the ongoing crisis in the image below.

headline: Stop Putting Girls Down and Start Listening To What Beyonce And Her Celebrity Friends Have To Say
lede:
I read a lot of "banning words is stupid!" type of comments flood my Facebook and Twitter feed when the #BanBossy campaign was launched by Lean In. But here's the deal: the focus should be on the bigger statement being made, and that is how many are using language and words like "bossy" in a derogatory way towards young girls who are simply asserting themselves. It may seem like a small issue to some, but the campaign is speaking to the young girls sitting in classrooms right now who are afraid to speak out, not to the cynical internet commenters.

So to the young girls online reading this: Beyoncé, Condoleezza Rice & Jane Lynch have your back if you wana go ahead and speak up.

headline: These Are Photos Of What Death Row Inmates Requested As Their Last Meal
lede:
If you had just one day left on earth, what would your last meal be?

Henry Hargreaves photographed what death row prisoners in America requested as their last meal in his "No Seconds" series, saying that his main goal "was to have the viewer identify with the prisoner though their meal request. I wanted the viewer to think of them as a person for a moment instead of them being anonymous."

I admire that Henry's photography project doesn't make a judgement the prisoners crime, but rather he tries to humanize the individual by showing subtle glimpses of the prisoners character and personality through their last meal choice.

headline: 'The Walking Dead' and 'Harry Potter' Stars Agree That Bankers Bonuses Are Bullshit
lede:
Bankers bonuses have hit the 80 billion barrier since the 2008 financial crisis. Yep I said billion there. How can we realistically try and tackle some of this gross inequality? The Robin Hood Tax sounds like a good start. Backed by a number of top dog financiers, Bill Gates and even the Vatican, it is a "tiny tax on share, bond and derivative transactions carried out by banks and hedge funds known as a financial transaction tax" and a lot of countries in Europe are currently talking about having this tax. Yay for smart ideas that address the serious imbalance of wealth!

Watch these Walking Dead, Harry Potter, and film stars act as country leaders and take a look at what the world might be like in 2024 with this tax in place and adopted by a bunch of countries... except my country, England.

headline: If Classic Movies Were Recast With Black People, Would They Still Be Classic?
lede:
I think the fact that this looks so new and unfamiliar (even to someone like me) brings up something to think about: Hollywood casting is ... well ... not so colorful.

Think, if Audrey Hepburn were black, would she have been in "Breakfast at Tiffany's"? If you're saying to yourself, "Surely her talent would have made her a success," think about how many classic movies Lena Horne or Dorothy Dandridge were in. And if Jada Pinkett-Smith's character in "The Matrix" was the lead (and not a supporting character), would we have cared about the movie as much? When stuff like this is the norm: ask yourself why we can't we have movie classics with leading black women where she doesn't play a slave or a maid?

These absolutely gorgeous images by Senegalese photographer Omar Victor Diop and French-American photographer Antoine Tempé have got me thinking as I get lost in the beauty.

lede:
What's that over there? Is that two large building blocks in the middle of Milan covered in a rich, green forest? Why yes, yes it is.

Or in other terms: lots and lots of trees in a tiny, little space to make the place look prettier. An ace, creative idea.

headline: Welcome To Solitary Confinement U.S. Style

Though it was originally written by someone else as a protest song of sorts, this is one of those gems that a singer just takes and totally owns from the start. “Strange Fruit” was shocking to many people when it came out originally in 1939. Even Ms. Holiday herself was initially reluctant to sing it, fearing retribution. Though many people knew that lynchings of African Americans in the South were relatively common, there was much resistance to ending it, since it was a very effective means of social control and political intimidation by Southern whites.

Because the song was so powerful and poignant for Holiday, there were some rules when she performed it: she would close the evening with the song, the waiters would stop service when the song began, and the room would be in total darkness except for a spotlight on Billie Holiday’s face. And there would be no encore.

Her voice is strong and impressive in this clip, but just look at the incredible expressiveness in her eyes as she gets through the haunting lyrics.

Trigger warning: lyrics about racial violence.

headline: The Super Bowl And A Bunch Of Little Girls Got Together And The Result Was Sciencetacular
lede:
The Problem: Fewer than 3 in 10 graduates in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM fields) are women. And barely 1 in 10 actual engineers are women.

One Solution: 2 years ago, an engineer named Debbie Sterling launched a Kickstarter campaign to make toys that helped little girls take an interest in STEM fields.

Using stories instead of instructions to guide them to build simple machines, the campaign was a great success, and Upworthy fans raised $100,000 beyond what Debbie had already raised. A year later, they made an amazing ad that 12 million more of you watched. And apparently many of you voted for them in Intuit's Small Business Big Game commercial contest, as they ended up winning the opportunity to air an entirely new commercial at the Super Bowl, where over 100 million people got to meet them.

Take a look at the long version of the commercial. And then go encourage your daughters to build things.

headline: Here’s Pete Seeger Doing One Of The Songs He Loved So Much
lede:
I saw Pete Seeger in Seattle about 15 years ago, with Ani DiFranco and several other musicians; they did a version of “We Shall Overcome” that absolutely stunned the entire concert hall, with everybody holding hands and singing along in one of those powerful and electric moments that can happen when humans connect over music.

This clip is from the 2009 inauguration ceremony of newly-elected President Obama. Pete Seeger came to play a little music with Bruce Springsteen, Seeger’s grandson Tao, and many others. Originally written by Woody Guthrie, who Seeger performed with many times, it’s a powerful version of “This Land Is Your Land,” with lyrics (including the frequently-forgotten last few stanzas!) below the video. As always, Pete tried to get the crowd to sing along, shouting out the lyrics so they could all join in.

We’ll miss you, Pete.

lede:

How ridiculous is it that people who should be working for us are instead acting like a bunch of frat bros pranking each other? That's Springteen and Fallon come in. I'm loving how this icon of New Jersey is highlighting that how preposterous this whole situation actually is.

headline: Hear The Inspiring Way The "The Worlds Ugliest Woman" Beat Her Bullies
lede:
How do you define beauty? Supermodels? Celebrities? Actually, a different question for you. What defines you?

Lizzie Velasquez was born with a rare condition that keeps her from gaining any weight. She's also blind in her right eye. When Lizzie was just a teen, she was the subject of the online video that described her as "the Worlds Ugliest Woman" and she was attacked by bullies telling her she should commit suicide. But she decided to fight back and not let her bullies define who she is.

Listen to how she describes how she created her own definitions of what she defines as beauty and happiness, as it is truly inspiring to hear.

lede:

And to those that think rape jokes are just jokes and should be protected by free speech, something to consider: Almost one-third of all rape victims developed PTSD sometime during their lifetime; and more than one in ten rape victims still has PTSD today.

That's hundreds of thousands of rape victims that could be traumatised again because you want to laugh at something that really isn't that funny.

headline: A Woman Pointed Out Sexism And The Internet Exploded. But When A Dude Says It...
lede:
Ever hear someone point out something sexist about a movie and immediately get the response: "It's just a movie. Get over it"? ... Yeah, me too.

Well, breaking news, y'all: You can like something AND acknowledge that it has faults! No, that doesn't make you a bad fan! In fact, I'd argue that makes you a really, really good fan because you're challenging your favorite thing to DO BETTER — to stop relying on problematic tropes and actually try to create something new, fresh, and fun without marginalizing already marginalized groups. I mean, after all, what are we saying about our culture if we're not actively thinking about the media we consume?

And that's what happens here: At 3:41, some dudes try to burn down a woman's career because she pointed out some kinda messed up things about their favorite video game. Definitely stick around to 4:07 for the best response about the media we consume and, you know, actually thinking critically about it.

headline: A Moslty Awesome Commercial That Respects Women! Just Ignore The Awful Tagline At The End.
lede:
Snickers — yeah, the chocolate bar Snickers — have released the most confusing-interesting-feasibly feminist video i've seen. I started watching it and thought "Haha, this is great!" ...but then the tagline at 1:07 just made me shake my head and shout at my laptop "IT WOULD HAVE BEEN PERFECT IF YOU DIDN'T HAVE THAT TAGLINE IN IT BOOOOO." It basically reads: treat women with respect? Nah, just eat Snickers and your normal misogynistic self will return! What's even more sucky is that they make a sweeping generalization that all construction workers are cat-callers. So yeah, not great.

But *perhaps* I'm looking at this too deeply? In short: Catcalling isn't cool. Even yelling "nice" stuff to women randomly on the street isn't cool. But let's face it, Snickers isn't going to solve it, so while the ending of this ad kinda sucks, I still think the most part of it can be enjoyed.

headline: See The Inspiring And Iconic Women These Young Girls Are Dressed Up As
lede:
Who do you want little girls to look up to? Women who work hard and achieve great things, presumably?

Step in photographer Eunique Jones, who created the photography project 'Because Of Them, We Can', a year long project which has now focused on women's history month. Jones dressed these young girls below as influential, accomplished, and powerful figures of women’s history alongside a famous quote of theirs. Jones felt it was important to refute stereotypes and build the self-esteem of children by connecting them to "heroes past and present who have and continue to pave the way."

Jones also commented that, "each child needs this message, regardless of their hue... There are numerous issues that divide us, however, wouldn't it be great if worked together to inundate children all over with these messages of excellence, accomplishment and responsibility."

I love this creative project so, so much. Oh and some of the women below are also overlooked, so if you don't recognise a name, give them a Google and find out more about the inspiring women.

headline: Dads Can Be Embarrassing. And Occasionally Profound.
lede:
DISCLOSURE: I have a daughter. Someday, she will grow up and become a young woman , and probably want to date people. There's this awful lizard part of my brain that gets protective of her and imagines threatening others who might date her someday, 13 years from now. And while I get protective of my son too, I think differently about each. And it's totally a hypocritical and ridiculous double standard. Because if you raise your kids right, they'll make mistakes, but they'll be responsible and make good choices (hopefully.) Their gender is irrelevant to that. So I want to acknowledge that I'm aware of my rampant hypocrisy. I'm a dad. I'm a jackass. I'm learning how to fight it and hold myself to a higher standard.

Which brings me to Jesse Parent, a dad who says all the things that probably every parent has dealt with thinking all their lives. At 1:50, he disables his lizard brain. And at 2:42, he makes up for his first 2 minutes. Hilariously.

headline: Have You Ever Wondered Why Society Hates Fat People? What If It Didn’t Have To?
lede:
There is so much fat shaming in our society and yet it's something like 60% of Americans are fat. Fat shaming doesn't make people skinny, it just makes fat people feel terrible about themselves. And uh, this shouldn't be revolutionary to say, but regardless of the shape or health of a body, the person inside is a human being with feelings and dreams and hopes and aspirations who deserves to be treated with respect. What do we gain as a society by making fat people feel bad about themselves? Nothing. We gain nothing.

Fat is not lazy (skinny people can be lazy too). Fat is not unhealthy (skinny people can be unhealthy too). Fat is not ugly (skinny people can be ugly too and ugly is subjective, anyway). Fat is not evil (skinny people can be evil too). Fat is not slow (skinny people can be slow too). Fat is not an insult. We shouldn't ban people from calling people "fat". We should remind people that fat is not an insult, it's an adjective. And as you'll see in this kickass documentary trailer, fat is f*cking phenomenal.

headline: An Argument About Your Privacy That Is So Simple, A Little Kid Can Understand It
lede:
Our right to a free and open Internets has been under threat lately. The NSA — btw, that stands for the National Security Agency, which has the fancy responsibility of analyzing and acting upon security data — has gotten into the habit of spying on Americans with no justification (including 12 spies who were using NSA tools to spy on their significant others). No, I'm not kidding.

The FCC — btw, that stands for the Federal Communications Commission, which is supposed to regulate and protect our communications channels — just made it easier for big companies to control the speed at which you are allowed to access particular websites. For example, your Internet company (i.e., Comcast or Verizon) could turn into a tiered pay system. So instead of being like a public utility where everyone gets the same amount of water or electricity, Verizon could give Netflix faster access for a fee, but then the smaller start-up that wants to compete and couldn't afford it would get slower access.

The Internet has become one of the most important resources in our lives. It's a shared resource that all of us take part in. Government spying on it, and corporate interference in it are probably not things we want for the future. So Mozilla had some children voice concern for their own future. Because it's kind of important. What kind of web do you want?

lede:

He finally let everyone know that his Grandparents came to this country legally, but they brought him here at age 5 and he never had gotten proper legal status. So he lived undocumented for most of his life. Jose came out in the national news and then decided to make a documentary about his journey and his fight to get rational immigration reform on the books in the United States.

That's when he met a self proclaimed "hardcore Republican" farmer named Lawrence. Lawrence has a far different perspective than much of his party when it comes to immigration. Here's why.

headline: Stephen Colbert Calls Out CNN On Their Inability To Report Actual News
lede:
Being a 24 hour news station is hard. You have find ways to fill 24 hours of airtime without being redundant and without there being breaking news every single day. For CNN, it's even tougher, because their bosses don't actually care about news quality, they care about ratings. They generally just let shrill politically partisan people scream past each other for half the day without fact checking them, and the other half, they underfund their actual reporters and do no long term investigative journalism. Instead, they find something sensationalist to milk and hype until it's been beaten to death with the tedious cudgel that is Wolf Blitzer's beard of indifference.

Stephen Colbert decided to get to the bottom of CNN's latest non-story, the story of if there was any story left about the tragic crash of a Malaysian Airlines plane. And calls them out quite brilliantly.

headline: It's Now Illegal For You & Some Friends To Sing, 'Joy To The World' At One State's Capitol
lede:
"Moral Monday" In North Carolina has been a regular gathering of people at the State Capitol, and people who come to it with signs and banners sing and chant to protest some of the really backwards things the legislature has been passing there. Rather than allow this rather insidious form of democracy, a law was passed ("Imminent Disturbance") that bans anyone from singing and chanting in a way that “disturbs” the daily business of the legislature. I can see the idea already spreading to states where out-of-control politicians are lusting after the “right” to shut us all up.

Those who began this great nation, and those who helped shaped it along the way, are rolling in their graves right now. Or perhaps they’re breaking out the megaphones and lyrics and they will descend on places that wish to silence the people, in groups of thousands of ghosts and spirits, haunting the demons who wish to drown democracy.

Sorry, that was a bit florid. I'm kinda passionate about this, as you can see...

headline: Why Do People Fuss Over Money In Politics? It's Only A Problem If You Don't Like Total Bullsh*t.
lede:
We can all tell when it's election season. Canvassers pour into our neighborhoods and public spaces. Campaign signs pop up on front yards, fences, windows, and buildings. Phones ring with volunteers (or robo-calls) eager to share how so-and-so candidate only wants the best for our country. Our favorite TV shows are interrupted by smear ads and soft-spoken placements that say, "Vote for me. I'm just like you." And, of course, there's the non-stop election coverage, which is ... well, no comment.

All of that costs money. So much of it that, in order to stand a chance at winning a senate seat, for example, a viable candidate can't waste time hearing from people who aren't major campaign donors, let alone folks who need and deserve more representation in the halls of Congress. The graphic below shows you what we're dealing with.

headline: Even If You Don't Know Someone With Parkinson's, You'll Think This Invention Is Pretty Darn Cool
lede: What if three times a day, just like clockwork, you felt overwhelmingly embarrassed and frustrated? If you're living with Parkinson's disease or another disorder that causes hand tremors, it's not a hypothetical. It's the daily experience of eating. Shaky hands make it nearly impossible to get food from plate to mouth without spilling - often on yourself. Able-bodied people like me don't have to think twice before picking up a knife and fork in front of people. So I'm glad to know inventions like this will make it easier for people with tremors to live happier lives with less effort and more dignity while we wait for a cure.

headline: Congress Silenced Her, But Jon Stewart Gave Her A Seriously Long Extended Interview
lede:
There’s a system out there that’s doing a good job of keeping sexual harassment A Thing That Exists. How? Somewhere out there, there’s something — A machine we should rage against, perhaps? — that is allowing sexual harassment to continue because not enough people are talking about it. How to fix this? Yep. We gotta talk about it. That can only mean one thing in this context — it's EXTENDED DAILY SHOW INTERVIEW TIME!

headline: In The Last 33 Years, 70 Of The 71 Mass-Murderers In The U.S. All Had 1 Thing In Common
lede:

headline: A Commercial That Almost Had Me Buying It's Product Until It Ruined Everything At The End
lede:
Snickers have released the most confusing-interesting-feasibly feminist video i've seen. Yeah, the chocolate bar Snickers. I started watching the video and thought "Haha, this is great!" ...but then the tagline at 1:07 just made me shake my head and shout at my laptop, "BOOOOO IT WOULD HAVE BEEN PERFECT IF YOU DIDN'T HAVE THAT TAGLINE IN IT." It basically reads: treat women with respect? Nah, just eat Snickers and your normal misogynistic self will return! What's even more sucky is that they make a sweeping generalization that all construction workers are cat-callers. If not eating Snickers means turning respectful and articulate, this is a terrible advert to get people to buy it.

But *perhaps* I'm looking at this too deeply. In short: Catcalling isn't cool. Even yelling "nice" stuff to women randomly on the street isn't cool. But let's face it, Snickers isn't going to solve it, so while the ending of this ad kinda sucks, I still think the most part of it can be enjoyed.

Every day women are harassed in the street simply by being a woman. Or in other words: every time we step out the house we run the risk of being shouted at, cat-called or assaulted usually in broad daylight. FUN!

headline: A Dad Gets A Standing Ovation For What He Says To Boys Who Want To Date His Daughter. Well Played.
lede:
DISCLOSURE: I have a daughter. Someday, she will grow up and become a young woman , and probably want to date people. There's this awful lizard part of my brain that gets protective of her and imagines threatening others who might date her someday, 13 years from now. And while I get protective of my son too, I think differently about each. And it's totally a hypocritical and ridiculous double standard. Because if you raise your kids right, they'll make mistakes, but they'll be responsible and make good choices (hopefully.) Their gender is irrelevant to that. So I want to acknowledge that I'm aware of my rampant hypocrisy. I'm a dad. I'm a jackass. I'm learning how to fight it and hold myself to a higher standard.

Which brings me to Jesse Parent, a dad who says all the things that probably every parent has dealt with thinking all their lives. At 1:50, he disables his lizard brain. And at 2:42, he makes up for his first 2 minutes. Hilariously.

headline: A Funny Commercial That Actually Respects Women! Oh, Except The Tagline At The End.
lede:
Snickers — yeah, the chocolate bar Snickers — have released the most confusing-interesting-feasibly feminist video i've seen. I started watching it and thought "Haha, this is great!" ...but then the tagline at 1:07 just made me shake my head and shout at my laptop "IT WOULD HAVE BEEN PERFECT IF YOU DIDN'T HAVE THAT TAGLINE IN IT BOOOOO." It basically reads: treat women with respect? Nah, just eat Snickers and your normal misogynistic self will return! What's even more sucky is that they make a sweeping generalization that all construction workers are cat-callers. So yeah, not great.

But *perhaps* I'm looking at this too deeply? In short: Catcalling isn't cool. Even yelling "nice" stuff to women randomly on the street isn't cool. But let's face it, Snickers isn't going to solve it, so while the ending of this ad kinda sucks, I still think the most part of it can be enjoyed.

headline: In The Last 33 Years, 70 Of The 71 Mass-Murderers In The U.S. All Had 1 Thing In Common
lede:
They were all men. Beyond that, most of them felt they were somehow being denied something that they should have been given. That attitude didn't appear out of thin air. It was honed by our culture, generation after generation, perpetuating bad ideas and stereotypes over time. Elliot Rodger is just the latest permutation of the guy who thinks that he is owed something and demands retribution. Rather that figure out that maybe he might not be communicating with women properly, he blamed their lack of interest on them.

The vast majority of men aren't evil, though. It does us no good to vilify an entire gender. Our culture that perpetuates it, on the other hand, needs to be scrutinized.

headline: This Father Has Something To Say To The Boys Who Want To Date His Daughter. Well Played.
lede:
DISCLOSURE: I have a daughter. Someday, she will grow up and become a young woman , and probably want to date people. There's this awful lizard part of my brain that gets protective of her and imagines threatening others who might date her someday, 13 years from now. And while I get protective of my son too, I think differently about each. And it's totally a hypocritical and ridiculous double standard. Because if you raise your kids right, they'll make mistakes, but they'll be responsible and make good choices (hopefully.) Their gender is irrelevant to that. headline: You Chose To Live In Ikea Homes – These People Do Not
lede:

In comes, erm, Ikea. Recognising that The UN Refugee Agency hasn't advanced their tents over the years, Ikea partnered with UNHCR to create smart, flatpack housing designed in an easy-to-trasport-and-set-up Ikea kinda way.

It's still at it's prototype stage, but it's smart design like this that could make a huge difference.

headline: See The Inspiring And Iconic Women These Young Girls Are Dressed Up As
lede:
Who do you want little girls to look up to? Women who work hard and achieve great things, presumably?

Step in photographer Eunique Jones, who created the photography project 'Because Of Them, We Can', a year long project which has now focused on women's history month. Jones dressed these young girls below as influential, accomplished, and powerful figures of women’s history alongside a famous quote of theirs. Jones felt it was important to refute stereotypes and build the self-esteem of children by connecting them to "heroes past and present who have and continue to pave the way."

Jones also commented that, "each child needs this message, regardless of their hue... There are numerous issues that divide us, however, wouldn't it be great if worked together to inundate children all over with these messages of excellence, accomplishment and responsibility."

I love this creative project so, so much. Oh and some of the women below are also overlooked, so if you don't recognise a name, give them a Google and find out more about the inspiring women.

headline: A Law Professor Gives Billionaires Who Try To Buy American Elections A Taste Of Their Own Medicine
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

headline: Stephen Colbert Calls Out CNN On Their Inability To Report Actual News

headline: A Law Professor Gives Billionaires Who Try To Buy American Elections A Taste Of Their Own Medicine
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.
