headline: Look At All The Ways Pop Culture Discriminates Against A Certain Body Type. How Wrong Is That?
lede:
There is so much fat shaming in our society and yet it's something like 60% of Americans are fat. Fat shaming doesn't make people skinny, it just makes fat people feel terrible about themselves. And uh, this shouldn't be revolutionary to say, but regardless of the shape or health of a body, the person inside is a human being with feelings and dreams and hopes and aspirations who deserves to be treated with respect. What do we gain as a society by making fat people feel bad about themselves? Nothing. We gain nothing.

Fat is not lazy (skinny people can be lazy too). Fat is not unhealthy (skinny people can be unhealthy too). Fat is not ugly (skinny people can be ugly too and ugly is subjective, anyway). Fat is not evil (skinny people can be evil too). Fat is not slow (skinny people can be slow too). Fat is not an insult. We shouldn't ban people from calling people "fat". We should remind people that fat is not an insult, it's an adjective. And as you'll see in this kickass documentary trailer, fat is f*cking phenomenal.

headline: Billie Holiday With One Of The Most Powerful And Emotional Performances Ever Captured On Video
lede:
Though it was originally written by someone else as a protest song of sorts, this is one of those gems that a singer just takes and totally owns from the start. “Strange Fruit” was shocking to many people when it came out originally in 1939. Even Ms. Holiday herself was initially reluctant to sing it, fearing retribution. Though many people knew that lynchings of African Americans in the South were relatively common, there was much resistance to ending it, since it was a very effective means of social control and political intimidation by Southern whites.

Because the song was so powerful and poignant for Holiday, there were some rules when she performed it: she would close the evening with the song, the waiters would stop service when the song began, and the room would be in total darkness except for a spotlight on Billie Holiday’s face. And there would be no encore.

Her voice is strong and impressive in this clip, but just look at the incredible expressiveness in her eyes as she gets through the haunting lyrics.

Trigger warning: lyrics about racial violence.

headline: A Law Professor Gives Billionaires Who Try To Buy American Elections A Taste Of Their Own Medicine
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

headline: These Women Posted This Photo On Facebook - But Unlike Most, They'll Face Torture For It
lede:

Masih asked Iranian women to send photos of themselves not wearing the veils. This may seem like a small thing to some, but in Iran, this is a bold statement against the government who are fixated on the way women dress, and require that they dress "modesty" — if they remove their veils in public, they can receive 70 lashes or 60 days in prison.

Masih says herself that she asked women to send "selfies of their private moments of freedom” — the campaign then led to 30,000 likes in its first five days.

headline: This Father Has Something To Say To The Boys Who Want To Date His Daughter. Well Played.
lede:
DISCLOSURE: I have a daughter. Someday, she will grow up and become a young woman , and probably want to date people. There's this awful lizard part of my brain that gets protective of her and imagines threatening others who might date her someday, 13 years from now. And while I get protective of my son too, I think differently about each. And it's totally a hypocritical and ridiculous double standard. Because if you raise your kids right, they'll make mistakes, but they'll be responsible and make good choices (hopefully.) Their gender is irrelevant to that. So I want to acknowledge that I'm aware of my rampant hypocrisy. I'm a dad. I'm a jackass. I'm learning how to fight it and hold myself to a higher standard.

Which brings me to Jesse Parent, a dad who says all the things that probably every parent has dealt with thinking all their lives. At 1:50, he disables his lizard brain. And at 2:42, he makes up for his first 2 minutes. Hilariously.

headline: Stephen Colbert Calls Out Cable News On It's Inability To Report Actual News
lede:
Being a 24 hour news station is hard. You have find ways to fill 24 hours of airtime without being redundant and without there being breaking news every single day. For CNN, it's even tougher, because their bosses don't actually care about news quality, they care about ratings. They generally just let shrill politically partisan people scream past each other for half the day without fact checking them, and the other half, they underfund their actual reporters and do no long term investigative journalism. Instead, they find something sensationalist to milk and hype until it's been beaten to death with the tedious cudgel that is Wolf Blitzer's beard of indifference.

Stephen Colbert decided to get to the bottom of their latest non-story, the story of if there was any story left about the tragedy on the crash of a Malaysian Airlines plane. He nails it.

headline: A Law Professor Gives Billionaires Who Try To Buy American Elections A Taste Of Their Own Medicine
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

One Solution: 2 years ago, an engineer named Debbie Sterling launched a Kickstarter campaign to make toys that helped little girls take an interest in STEM fields.

Using stories instead of instructions to guide them to build simple machines, the campaign was a great success, and Upworthy fans raised $100,000 beyond what Debbie had already raised. A year later, they made an amazing ad that 12 million more of you watched. And apparently many of you voted for them in Intuit's Small Business Big Game commercial contest, as they ended up winning the opportunity to air an entirely new commercial at the Super Bowl, where over 100 million people got to meet them.

Take a look at the long version of the commercial. And then go encourage your daughters to build things.

headline: A Law Professor Gives Billionaires Who Try To Buy American Elections A Taste Of Their Own Medicine
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

headline: Don't Look Now, But Our Country Is In A Place It Hasn't Been For Well Over 100 Years
lede:
A few definitions to tee this up:

Oligarchy: A society where power is in the hands of very few people, usually determined by wealth, corporate and family ties, and the military.

The Gilded Age: From the 1870s to the 1900s, our country was run by very few people (think John D. Rockefeller, J.P. Morgan, Andrew W. Mellon, Andrew Carnegie) but also marked by extreme poverty. The term was coined by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner to mean, "an era of serious social problems disguised by thin gold gilding."

So ... are we there yet?!

headline: Stephen Colbert Explains More In 5 Minutes About How Bad Cable News Is Than Cable News Really Could
lede:
Being a 24 hour news station is hard. You have find ways to fill 24 hours of airtime without being redundant and without there being breaking news every single day. For CNN, it's even tougher, because their bosses don't actually care about news quality, they care about ratings. They generally just let shrill politically partisan people scream past each other for half the day without fact checking them, and the other half, they underfund their actual reporters and do no long term investigative journalism. Instead, they find something sensationalist to milk and hype until it's been beaten to death with the tedious cudgel that is Wolf Blitzer's beard of indifference.

Stephen Colbert decided to get to the bottom of their latest non-story, the story of if there was any story left about the tragedy on the crash of a Malaysian Airlines plane. He nails it.

lede:

Masih asked Iranian women to send photos of themselves not wearing the veils. This may seem like a small thing to some, but in Iran, this is a bold statement against the government who are fixated on the way women dress, and require that they dress "modesty" — if they remove their veils in public, they can receive 70 lashes or 60 days in prison.

Masih says herself that she asked women to send "selfies of their private moments of freedom” — the campaign then led to 30,000 likes in its first five days.

excerpt: What words like ‘Gilded Age’ and ‘Oligarchy’ really mean to us today.
headline: Don't Look Now, But Our Country Is In A Place It Hasn't Been For Well Over 100 Years
lede:
A few definitions to tee this up:

Oligarchy: A society where power is in the hands of very few people, usually determined by wealth, corporate and family ties, and the military.

The Gilded Age: From the 1870s to the 1900s, our country was run by very few people (think John D. Rockefeller, J.P. Morgan, Andrew W. Mellon, Andrew Carnegie) but also marked by extreme poverty. The term was coined by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner to mean, "an era of serious social problems disguised by thin gold gilding."

So ... are we there yet?!

headline: See The Inspiring And Iconic Women These Young Girls Are Dressed Up As
lede:
Who do you want little girls to look up to? Women who work hard and achieve great things, presumably?

Step in photographer Eunique Jones, who created the photography project 'Because Of Them, We Can', a year long project which has now focused on women's history month. Jones dressed these young girls below as influential, accomplished, and powerful figures of women’s history alongside a famous quote of theirs. Jones felt it was important to refute stereotypes and build the self-esteem of children by connecting them to "heroes past and present who have and continue to pave the way."

Jones also commented that, "each child needs this message, regardless of their hue... There are numerous issues that divide us, however, wouldn't it be great if worked together to inundate children all over with these messages of excellence, accomplishment and responsibility."

I love this creative project so, so much. Oh and some of the women below are also overlooked, so if you don't recognise a name, give them a Google and find out more about the inspiring women.

headline: If You Recognize The Woman Character Trope Described Here, You'll Shake Your Head Too

Watching it, you'll find yourself going "oh I recognise all of this!" and you'll be able to spot it a mile off when watching a movie in the future.

headline: Say What You Will About Fat Bodies, The People Inside Them Sure Do Deserve Respect
lede:
There is so much fat shaming in our society and yet it's something like 60% of Americans are fat. Fat shaming doesn't make people skinny, it just makes fat people feel terrible about themselves. And uh, this shouldn't be revolutionary to say, but regardless of the shape or health of a body, the person inside is a human being with feelings and dreams and hopes and aspirations who deserves to be treated with respect. What do we gain as a society by making fat people feel bad about themselves? Nothing. We gain nothing.

Fat is not lazy (skinny people can be lazy too). Fat is not unhealthy (skinny people can be unhealthy too). Fat is not ugly (skinny people can be ugly too and ugly is subjective, anyway). Fat is not evil (skinny people can be evil too). Fat is not slow (skinny people can be slow too). Fat is not an insult. We shouldn't ban people from calling people "fat". We should remind people that fat is not an insult, it's an adjective. And as you'll see in this kickass documentary trailer, fat is f*cking phenomenal.

headline: NEWSFLASH: You Can Be A Fat Person And Be F*cking Phenomenal
lede:
There is so much fat shaming in our society and yet it's something like 60% of Americans are fat. Fat shaming doesn't make people skinny, it just makes fat people feel terrible about themselves. And uh, this shouldn't be revolutionary to say, but regardless of the shape or health of a body, the person inside is a human being with feelings and dreams and hopes and aspirations who deserves to be treated with respect. What do we gain as a society by making fat people feel bad about themselves? Nothing. We gain nothing.

Fat is not lazy (skinny people can be lazy too). Fat is not unhealthy (skinny people can be unhealthy too). Fat is not ugly (skinny people can be ugly too and ugly is subjective, anyway). Fat is not evil (skinny people can be evil too). Fat is not slow (skinny people can be slow too). Fat is not an insult. We shouldn't ban people from calling people "fat". We should remind people that fat is not an insult, it's an adjective. And as you'll see in this kickass documentary trailer, fat is f*cking phenomenal.

headline: Banksy Has Replaced His Famous Artwork With A Syrian Girl

headline: Don't Look Now, But Our Country Is In A Place It Hasn't Been For Well Over 100 Years
lede:
A few definitions to tee this up:

Oligarchy: A society where power is in the hands of very few people, usually determined by wealth, corporate and family ties, and the military.

The Gilded Age: From the 1870s to the 1900s, our country was run by very few people (think John D. Rockefeller, J.P. Morgan, Andrew W. Mellon, Andrew Carnegie) but also marked by extreme poverty. The term was coined by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner to mean, "an era of serious social problems disguised by thin gold gilding."

So ... are we there yet?!

headline: Billie Holiday With One Of The Most Powerful And Emotional Performances Ever Captured On Video
lede:
Though it was originally written by someone else as a protest song of sorts, this is one of those gems that a singer just takes and totally owns from the start. “Strange Fruit” was shocking to many people when it came out originally in 1939. Even Ms. Holiday herself was initially reluctant to sing it, fearing retribution. Though many people knew that lynchings of African Americans in the South were relatively common, there was much resistance to ending it, since it was a very effective means of social control and political intimidation by Southern whites.

Because the song was so powerful and poignant for Holiday, there were some rules when she performed it: she would close the evening with the song, the waiters would stop service when the song began, and the room would be in total darkness except for a spotlight on Billie Holiday’s face. And there would be no encore.

Her voice is strong and impressive in this clip, but just look at the incredible expressiveness in her eyes as she gets through the haunting lyrics.

Trigger warning: lyrics about racial violence.

headline: It's Now Illegal For You & Some Friends To Sing, 'Joy To The World' At One State's Capitol
lede:
"Moral Monday" In North Carolina has been a regular gathering of people at the State Capitol, and people who come to it with signs and banners sing and chant to protest some of the really backwards things the legislature has been passing there. Rather than allow this rather insidious form of democracy, a law was passed ("Imminent Disturbance") that bans anyone from singing and chanting in a way that “disturbs” the daily business of the legislature. I can see the idea already spreading to states where out-of-control politicians are lusting after the “right” to shut us all up.

Those who began this great nation, and those who helped shaped it along the way, are rolling in their graves right now. Or perhaps they’re breaking out the megaphones and lyrics and they will descend on places that wish to silence the people, in groups of thousands of ghosts and spirits, haunting the demons who wish to drown democracy.

Sorry, that was a bit florid. I'm kinda passionate about this, as you can see...

headline: A Bunch Of Little Scientists Sing An Epic Power Ballad And Rock Out At The Super Bowl
lede:
The Problem: Fewer than 3 in 10 graduates in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM fields) are women. And barely 1 in 10 actual engineers are women.

One Solution: 2 years ago, an engineer named Debbie Sterling launched a Kickstarter campaign to make toys that helped little girls take an interest in STEM fields.

Using stories instead of instructions to guide them to build simple machines, the campaign was a great success, and Upworthy fans raised $100,000 beyond what Debbie had already raised. A year later, they made an amazing ad that 12 million more of you watched. And apparently many of you voted for them in Intuit's Small Business Big Game commercial contest, as they ended up winning the opportunity to air an entirely new commercial at the Super Bowl, where over 100 million people got to meet them.

Take a look at the long version of the commercial. And then go encourage your daughters to build things.

Oligarchy: A society where power is in the hands of very few people, usually determined by wealth, corporate and family ties, and the military.

headline: It's Now Illegal For You & Some Friends To Sing, 'Joy To The World' At One State's Capitol
lede:

I can see the idea already spreading to states where out-of-control politicians are lusting after the “right” to shut us all up.

Those who began this great nation, and those who helped shaped it along the way, are rolling in their graves right now. Or perhaps they’re breaking out the megaphones and lyrics and they will descend on places that wish to silence the people, in groups of thousands of ghosts and spirits, haunting the demons who wish to drown democracy.

headline: How To Live Like You're On A Farm When You're Nowhere Near One
lede:
A couple years back I had the privilege of caring for a bunch of chickens as part of a community-run chicken coop. Mostly it was getting up at sunrise and mucking around in my boots, but it was also fun to interact with them, and I always felt a vaguely child-like awe when I checked for eggs in the straw.

Now, the odd part of all this is that I rarely eat eggs. So, I sold mine instead of keeping them. I just liked hanging out with those little guys. And I have perfected my impression of a chicken running ... so ... there's that. What I'm trying to say is, chickens are cool creatures to have. Maybe the info below will help you decide if getting a few is right for you. :)

headline: Here's A Graphic That Made Me Feel Insignificant. Until I Remembered I'm Far From Alone.
lede:
We can all tell when it's election season. Canvassers pour into our neighborhoods and public spaces. Campaign signs pop up on front yards, fences, windows, and buildings. Phones ring with volunteers (or robo-calls) eager to share how so-and-so candidate only wants the best for our country. Our favorite TV shows are interrupted by smear ads and soft-spoken placements that say, "Vote for me. I'm just like you." And, of course, there's the non-stop election coverage, which is ... well, no comment.

All of that costs money. So much of it that, in order to stand a chance at winning a senate seat, for example, a viable candidate can't waste time hearing from people who aren't major campaign donors, let alone folks who need and deserve more representation in the halls of Congress. The graphic below shows you what we're dealing with.

headline: In 1991, Congress Assumed That Sexual Harassment Happened, But They Refused To Say That It Mattered
lede:

Yep. We gotta talk about it. That can only mean one thing in this context — it's EXTENDED DAILY SHOW INTERVIEW TIME!

This is Anita Hill, one of the many women leading this rage against the machine by refusing to stop talking about sexual harassment until there’s absolutely nothing left to talk about. In part 1 she lays out her plan for what's next in this fight, and in part 2 she bravely inspires everyone with her principles and positivity.

headline: A Law Professor Gives Billionaires Who Try To Buy American Elections A Taste Of Their Own Medicine
lede:
How bad has the money in politics situation gotten? A new study by researchers at Princeton and Northwestern found that, and I'm quoting directly here: "When the preferences of economic elites and the stands of organized interest groups are controlled for, the preferences of the average American appear to have only a minuscule, near-zero, statistically non-significant impact upon public policy.”

In other words: If you can't afford to hire a lobbyist or raise money for politicians, your opinion literally does not matter.

But don't go into a hopeless despair spiral just yet. On May 1st, Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig launched Mayday PAC: A crowdfunded Super PAC with the sole mission of forcing Congress to get money out of politics. The response so far has been overwhelming: They've raised over half a million dollars in the first week alone.

Oligarchy: A society where power is in the hands of very few people, usually determined by wealth, corporate and family ties, and the military.

The Gilded Age: From the 1870s to the 1900s, our country was very much run by very few people (think John D. Rockefeller, J.P. Morgan, Andrew W. Mellon, Andrew Carnegie) but also marked by extreme poverty. The term was coined by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner to mean, "an era of serious social problems disguised by thin gold gilding."

So ... are we there yet?!

lede:

Rather than allow this rather insidious form of democracy, a law was passed ("Imminent Disturbance") that bans anyone from singing and chanting in a way that “disturbs” the daily business of the legislature. I can see the idea already spreading to states where out-of-control politicians are lusting after the “right” to shut us all up.

Those who began this great nation, and those who helped shaped it along the way, are rolling in their graves right now. Or perhaps they’re breaking out the megaphones and lyrics and they will descend on places that wish to silence the people, in groups of thousands of ghosts and spirits, haunting the demons who wish to drown democracy.

headline: It's Now Illegal For You & Some Friends To Sing, 'Joy To The World' At One State's Capitol
lede:

Rather than allow this rather insidious form of democracy, a law was passed ("Imminent Disturbance") that bans anyone from singing and chanting in a way that “disturbs” the daily business of the legislature. I can see the idea already spreading to states where out-of-control politicians are lusting after the “right” to shut us all up.

Those who began this great nation, and those who helped shaped it along the way, are rolling in their graves right now. Or perhaps they’re breaking out the megaphones and lyrics and they will descend on places that wish to silence the people, in groups of thousands of ghosts and spirits, haunting the demons who wish to drown democracy.

That factory us about to be torn down, but there’s a group of people working frantically to try to purchase a small part of the plant and turn it into a museum. headline: We Have A Big Problem — And I'm Not Sure That Voting Can Fix It
lede:
We can all tell when it's election season. Canvassers pour into our neighborhoods and public spaces. Campaign signs pop up on front yards, fences, windows, and buildings. Phones ring with volunteers (or robo-calls) eager to share how so-and-so candidate only wants the best for our country. Our favorite TV shows are interrupted by smear ads and soft-spoken placements that say, "Vote for me. I'm just like you." And, of course, there's the non-stop election coverage, which is ... well, no comment.

All of that costs money. So much of it that, in order to stand a chance at winning a senate seat, for example, a viable candidate can't waste time hearing from people who aren't major campaign donors, let alone folks who need and deserve more representation in the halls of Congress. The graphic below shows you what we're dealing with.

headline: See The Incredible Women Of Color Honored By These Girls In This Adorable Set Of Portraits
lede:
All young people deserve inspiring women to look up to – and young girls of color have some incredible women to look up to, as shown in this wonderful project 'Because Of Them We Can' by Eunique Jones Gibson. Below are just eighteen of the many portraits Eunique has taken of young boys and girls dressed as inspiring, accomplished people.

But Eunique isn't simply dressing cute children up here as well-known leaders, thinkers and artists: she's inspiring a new generation to believe in themselves. Eunique commented that she wanted children to immerse themselves with these messages of excellence, accomplishment and responsibility, and stated that the project is "committed as ever before to encourage and empower people of all ages and hues to dream out loud and reimagine themselves as greater than they are, simply by connecting the dots between the past, the present and the future." Hear what she has to say in her own words in the video, and then see a small selection of posters below. After that, do yourself a favor and order a ton of her posters because they are just the *best*.

headline: Still Screwed By His Government, He's Found A Way To Survive
lede:
Burma has a long riddled history of repression, and even though we've seen the country taking progressive steps towards freedom in recent years, a lot of people are like "Er, keep your eyes open world, this is just cosmetic change — there's still a ton of political prisoners, in-discriminative killings of ethnic groups, and no freedom to say out loud that the government is total shit."

This man below was imprisoned for his beliefs and for taking part in peaceful demonstrations. When he was released, there were so many barriers in place for him to live a normal life. Fortunately he and some other former political prisoners found this smart way of making an income *and* keep their story alive.

headline: The Saying 'Money Talks' Has Never Been More True
lede:
We can all tell when it's election season. Canvassers pour into our neighborhoods and public spaces. Campaign signs pop up on front yards, fences, windows, and buildings. Phones ring with volunteers (or robo-calls) eager to share how so-and-so candidate only wants the best for our country. Our favorite TV shows are interrupted by smear ads and soft-spoken placements that say, "Vote for me. I'm just like you." And, of course, there's the non-stop election coverage, which is ... well, no comment.

All of that costs money. So much of it that, in order to stand a chance at winning a senate seat, for example, a viable candidate can't waste time hearing from people who aren't major campaign donors, let alone folks who need and deserve more representation in the halls of Congress. The graphic below shows you what we're dealing with.

headline: Ever Heard of "Environmental Justice Populations"? It's What The State Department Calls Poor People.
lede: Okay, so here's the deal. I grew up in WV, where all the mineral wealth gets extracted by out-of-state companies. They bring in professionals for a few years to get stuff set up, and then they jet. Locals don't get much money out of it--just acid streams, dangerous jobs, and black lung. But you know, they need those jobs. A bad job is better than no job. You gotta eat. The latest report from the State Dept.* shows that the Keystone XL Pipeline will be pretty much the same deal, but in Montana. All is not yet lost--your friends in the US Senate haven't quite decided if they're giving this the green light. Write to your senators! It's not too late.

Trigger warning: Discussion of rape, sexual assault, abuse.

Almost every survivor of sexual assault or abuse will at one point think, "It was my fault."

What many of us don't know is WHY survivors feel shame and guilt, or why others around them might blame them instead of the perpetrator. The following cartoon breaks down the reasons why.

So, to all the survivors out there who are blaming themselves for what happened, here's the psychology behind why you might feel so guilty. I'm crossing my fingers that at least a couple of you will read this and finally feel some solace.

And for anyone who has ever asked, "Why didn't she run away?" or "Why didn't he scream?" This one's for you, too.

headline: I Didn’t Know I Was A 'Cyber Utopian' But After Watching This Clip, I’m Not Anymore
lede:
At a time where we are all connected by social networks and we watch revolutions unfold on Twitter hours before they’re splashed all over TV news, it’s easy to assume that the only thing a movement really needs is the internet. The truth is actually much more complex as Evgeny Morozov illustrates (pun intended) with the help of some cats and mice.

He gives some background, then discusses online debate in politically oppressive countries at 3:50, but he shocked me right after the 5-minute mark. You need to know how some governments are using the internet to track down activists and dissenters. There are no cookie cutter approaches to changing the world.

headline: How And Why We Use 'Sorry' Fuels Gender Stereotypes, And This Shampoo Ad Calls It Out
lede:
There’s nothing wrong with apologizing. In fact, it’s sort of what you’re supposed to do when you’re in the wrong. However, studies show that women are more likely to apologize for non-offensive behavior than men… Which unfortunately fuels the double-standard that women who aren’t “apologetic enough” are bossy (...or worse).

So, ladies and gentlemen. I’m not here to tell you how to use your words... That would be silly. But I am here to show you this video, in hopes that we might recognize this behavior in ourselves and work together to create a world in which these sorts of apologies aren’t expected from either gender.

In its ruling, it's basically stated that private businesses (public businesses still have to be decent human being corporate entities) can interfere with their employee's reproductive health.

John Oliver has an opinion about that. Especially at 3:40.

headline: Rich Kids Getting Financial Aid From Colleges Is The Single Most Annoying Thing I've Learned Today
lede:
I have conflicted thoughts about college. While I learned so much at my four years at Rhode Island School of Design, the tuition costs to go there are staggering (which frankly, is an understatement). The financial aid I received from RISD in addition to federal grants were much-welcomed silver linings, and I was able to attend, albeit with a debt-friend that will follow me around for a couple decades.

Marian Wang wonders: What happens, though, when a student is deemed "not worthy" of financial aid?

headline: 30 Seconds Of Women Apologizing, Followed By 30 Seconds Of *Not* Apologizing. Which Do You Prefer?
lede:
There’s nothing wrong with apologizing. In fact, it’s sort of what you’re supposed to do when you’re in the wrong. However, studies show that women are more likely to apologize for non-offensive behavior than men… Which unfortunately fuels the double-standard that women who aren’t “apologetic enough” are bossy (...or worse).

So, ladies and gentlemen. I’m not here to tell you how to use your words... That would be silly. But I am here to show you this video, in hopes that we might recognize this behavior in ourselves and work together to create a world in which these sorts of apologies aren’t expected from either gender.

headline: If You Thought Having Kids Was Too Hard To Be Worth It, You're Almost Right
lede:
You know what parents and mystics have in common? Every day feels like a hallucination. If you wonder why your mom friends actually say sentences like, "Please don't wipe your hands on the cat," Rabbi Dayna Ruttenberg offers a window into their world. Parenthood is rough from minute to minute, but Ruttenberg offers a way to see it as a chance to connect with the bigness of the universe.

At 3:45, Rabbi Ruttenberg offers a practical idea for stopping fights you're not going to win. At 8:00, we get a picture of what mystics might say about life with kids. And at 9:10, I learned that I'm not the only one who threatens to gobble up chubby little baby toes...and that there's a spiritual reason for my cannibal impulse.

headline: Rich Kids Can't Be All Bad, Right? Unless They All Do This To Poor People Before They Go To College.
lede:
While I learned so much at my four years at college, the tuition costs to go to Rhode Island School of Design are staggering. They were for me and my family, at least. I had classmates who seemed like their parents could send them to college a second time if they wanted to.

The financial aid I received from RISD in addition to federal grants were much-welcomed silver linings, and I was able to attend, after also taking out loans that will follow me around for a long, long time. Writer Marian Wang wonders: What happens, though, when a student is deemed "not worthy" of financial aid? And how does it happen?

headline: If You're One Of Those People Who Just Doesn't 'Get' Trans People, Here's An Easy Fix
lede:
I'm trying to get better about gender. Not just equality, but really understanding the alternatives to boxing other people in based on my perceptions of gender. But it's hard, right? It's hard to think about gender in any other way than what we've been taught from childhood: boys grow up to be men and girls grow up to be women. But it doesn't have to be hard.

This talk covers biological sex and gender identity really well in the beginning. Feel free to start from there, but I'm going start you about two-thirds through (10:03) where he begins talk about the aspect of gender we notice the most: gender expression. It's not all serious, I promise. There are some great laughs in there too.

headline: Here's The Special Word For When White People "Discover" Something
lede:
Once upon a time, Miley Cyrus twerked on TV, but Miley didn't invent twerking. Still, some people say she "discovered" it.

Once upon a time, Elvis sang rock n' roll, but he didn't invent it. Still, he's remembered as the father of rock n' roll.

And once upon a time, Columbus came to America, which already had already been inhabited for thousands of years. Today, we say he "discovered" America.

Well, folks, I just "discovered" a new term for all of this: Columbusing.

So ... do these CEOs deserve that much more?

headline: These 2 Minutes Of Frozen-In-Motion LEGO People Drilled Into My Heart And Struck Anger. A Lot Of It.
lede:
Think of your favorite toy from childhood. What color was it? Now think of that toy if it were sponsored by the first giant corporation that comes to mind. With all that branding, the company (and it's colors) become part of the toy itself. I gotta say, the idea that kids would grow up with the same fond memories I have for Pogs and Teddy Ruxpin for an oil corporation making use of the Halo effect? Very unnerving.

Is a toy with a big sponsored logo on it still a toy? Or is it a tool?

headline: Here's How Advertisements Might Look If They Stated The Things They Make Many People Feel
lede:
We're so inundated with images of "ideal" women that whether we intend for it to happen or not, those superficial images — and the ones we never see that might actually represent so many of us — can sometimes affect our feelings about our appearance and self-worth. I know the standard response is, "Well, don't let it bother you!" But that's easier said than done, particularly when we are bombarded with the standards from a very young age.

This photo series, called "Stop the Beauty Madness," is intended to start conversations about ageism, racism, fat shaming, body image, eating disorders, sexuality, and more — all the madness that we're presented with regularly thanks to today's beauty "ideals."

headline: 2 Teenagers Destroyed Countless Families. These Guys Rewound The Tape To Try To Answer Why.
lede:
Jamie and Geoff do writing workshops all over the country in prisons, juvenile halls, and high schools, seeking out the kids who have no outlet to express their rage and pain. From their work, they wrote a play, "In Spite of Everything," which toured around the globe and brought people together to discuss the uniquely horrific American tragedy that is school shootings. And from that play came this story.

Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold had three months left of school. Dylan had been accepted into a college program. There was a moment they could have called it all off and went on like nothing happened. But they didn't. They crossed the line no one should cross. Columbine was a horrific tragedy that made a lasting impact on America. It woke us all up, it made us remember there really is evil in the world, and it shook us to the core. Growing up in Colorado, I couldn't ever have imagined anyone doing this. And yet it happened. And all the adults missed it. And none of us could fathom why or how it was even possible.

Jamie DeWolf and Geoff Trenchard had fantasies like Dylan Klebold and Eric Harris growing up, too. Hell, any kid who was having a rough go would occasionally imagine what they'd do if they could. I know I did. But it never occurred to me to actually take any action. It was just fantasy. So what made them different? What made them say, "Let's go all the way with this"?

Jamie and Geoff tried to find out. They wanted to give a voice to alienated kids who don't make the horrible choices Dylan and Eric made. They wanted to discover what drove these kids to such angry places and find a healthy outlet to help kids like them survive.

They say some pretty shocking things in this, but I urge you to listen all the way through. It's pretty damn poignant.

TRIGGER WARNING: This re-enacts the tragic and violent events of that day and includes shootings and violence.

But I can't be proud that so many states celebrate fighting a war in order to keep people like me in chains – and spend tax dollars to do it.

headline: A Bank Lobbyist Tries To Make Excuses For A Bank That Took Advantage Of Some Orphans. Seriously.
lede:
When you file for bankruptcy, you can often get debt forgiven or restructured. But if you have student loans, some nice lobbyists have made sure they are not part of that deal. A mom with $100k in student loan debt died, and her children went into the care of their grandparents, who were then saddled with their dead child's debt and had no way to get the debt forgiven.

Senator Warren decided to ask one of the top lobbyists who run a consumer bank lobbying organization (for the banks, not the consumers) how and when he's going to fix that. It didn't go well for the banker. Especially at 5:20.

headline: Here's A List Of Insults Too Many Black People Know. Who's Saying Them Might Surprise You.
lede: I'll never forget in elementary school, coming back from a long weekend at the beach and my classmates calling me "burnt french toast" because my skin had gotten so dark. I remember being upset not just because they were making fun of my skin, but mostly because I really liked my skin and couldn't understand why being darker was suddenly a bad thing. The fact that black people come in so many shades is incredibly beautiful, but sadly has always come with it's own complications. This short documentary explores some of the stereotypes associated with different skin tones, along with the effects of colorism in the black community.

headline: A Guy Explains That 4 Of 6700 Banks Are Not Hurting Families. The Senator Responds Correctly.
lede:
When you file for bankruptcy, you can often get debt forgiven or restructured. But if you have student loans, some nice lobbyists have made sure they are not part of that deal. A mom with $100k in student loan debt died, and her children went into the care of their grandparents, who were then saddled with their dead child's debt and had no way to get the debt forgiven.

Senator Warren decided to ask one of the top lobbyists who run a consumer bank lobbying organization (for the banks, not the consumers) how and when he's going to fix that. It didn't go well for the banker. Especially at 5:20.

lede:

Bottom line — a woman's body and sexuality in some way were being commandeered without her say-so.

headline: Robin Williams' Advice For People Who Are Depressed Is Really Good
lede:
There's been a quote going around attributed to Robin Williams that goes as follows: "You're only given a little spark of madness. You mustn't lose it." Here's where it came from. He was performing at the ROXY for a brand new comedy special on a little known network called HBO. In the audience were a surprising group of people. Henry Winkler (The Fonz), Tony Danza before he was famous, and even John Ritter whom he does a weird round of improv with at the end of this video.

I've included just the moment that sort of kept me sane as a kid. It helped me justify how weird I was. It's a delightful 5 minutes. If you'd like to watch the whole special, excerpts of which were used to create his first album, "Reality... What A Concept" you can start it from the beginning.

I always wondered why history like this was never taught in school when I grew up. Could it be that the powers that be would rather keep this kind of thing under wraps?

headline: A 16-Year-Old Kid In Ferguson Says More With A Marker And A Piece Of Paper Than All The Media Did
lede: Most of the press coverage of the protesting after the Mike Brown shooting in Ferguson has centered around his character, personal issues, and a small number of looters rather than asking why people are mad. Much of the media is playing up the looting and rioting, ignoring the vast majority of protesters who are peaceful and standing up for their rights, and almost none of them are asking the question, "Why are people reacting like this?" If you want to get to the heart of why people are so frustrated and enraged, look no further than 14-year-old Shane Flowers, who expresses much of what people are struggling with at 1:47. At 3:27, he writes down the question that many in the community might be asking.

headline: In 1961, This Was Something That "Nice" People Didn't Talk About.
lede:
In 1961, Shirley Maclaine and Audrey Hepburn starred in The Children's Hour. While censorship guidelines at the time of filming didn't outrightly prohibit the mention of homosexuality, it was widely know that the topic was not something that was acceptable to discuss on the big screen.

At 2:20, you'll see the pain that came with Shirley Maclaine's character's struggle. As one of the first movies to broach this topic, you'll be very surprised to hear what she says at 2:50 and Susie Bright's insight at the end painfully illustrates the things our society still needs to work on.

headline: Maybe They Think It's OK To Abuse Them Because They Aren't REAL Women?
lede:
I'm an unabashed nerd. Most prominent in my repertoire of nerdery is video games. But video games haven't always been good to me. Female characters are routinely verbally and physically abused, sexually assaulted, and killed in video games. I'm always annoyed by unnecessarily revealing costumes and obnoxiously gigantic boobs, but it's the violence against female characters that keeps me away from certain games – even entire genres.

This video starts with a long series of graphic examples of unnecessary violence against women from 28 of the most successful video games of the last eight years*, but I'm starting you toward the end (23:30) where Anita Sarkeesian discusses an example of a video that does "abuse as a theme" right and why it's important (and possible) for video games to be violent without being harmful.

Quick vocab lesson before you start: "NPC" means "non-playable character".

If you start at 23:30 then there are no descriptions or depictions of violence, but if you start at the beginning instead – trigger warning like all get out for everything I mentioned above.

headline: She Got Tired Of People Cutting Down All Of The Trees, So She Decided To Live In One
lede:
With so many scary and questionable things going on in our environment today, it’s easy to sit with our hands crossed and juuust — be overwhelmed. Think one person can’t make a difference? Think again.

A woman got tired of seeing her favorite trees disappear, so she decided to move for 449 days to make a really important point.

headline: Women Can Look So Life-Like In Video Games. So Can The Way They Get Beaten To Death.
lede:
I'm an unabashed nerd. Most prominent in my repertoire of nerdery is video games. But video games haven't always been good to me. Female characters are routinely verbally and physically abused, sexually assaulted, and killed in video games. I'm always annoyed by unnecessarily revealing costumes and obnoxiously gigantic boobs, but it's the violence against female characters that keeps me away from certain games – even entire genres.

This video starts with a long series of graphic examples of unnecessary violence against women from 28 of the most successful video games of the last eight years*, but I'm starting you toward the end (23:30) where Anita Sarkeesian discusses an example of a video that does "abuse as a theme" right and why it's important (and possible) for video games to be violent without being harmful.

Quick vocab lesson before you start: "NPC" means "non-playable character".

If you start at 23:30 then there are no descriptions or depictions of violence, but if you start at the beginning instead – trigger warning like all get out for everything I mentioned above.

headline: Some Kids Are Getting Tobacco Poisoning, But How It’s Happening Is What’s Really Disturbing
lede:
Back in the days of family farming, everyone pitched in, and US Labor Laws reflects this mostly bygone reality. This hasn’t been lost on commercial farmers, who see laws that allow children of any age at all to work on small farms, and kids over 12 to work on a farm of any size. It’s a giant loophole you can drive a tractor through, and the tobacco industry is all over it. So is The Daily Show, fortunately.

If you’d like to learn more about this, there’s a great article about kids an tobacco farming at Human Rights Watch.
share_text: Will we ever run out of crazy?

headline: Her Feet Didn’t Touch The Ground For Over A Year,  Because Of Something That’s About 400 Years Old
lede:
With so many questionable things going on in our environment today, it’s easy to sit with our hands crossed and just be overwhelmed. Think one person can’t make a difference? Think again.

A woman got tired of seeing her favorite trees disappear, so she decided to relocate for 449 days to make a really important point.

Far from a snoozefest, this video surprised me by how engaging it is, plus it's really gorgeous. At 55 seconds in, she already had a tight grip on my heart strings. At 1:51 find out what’s got her in an uproar, and by 10:20 see why her courage means so much.

headline: If You Can't Do This In The Bedroom, You Might As Well Break Up With Your Partner Now
lede:
After my dad was diagnosed with Pancreatic cancer, we had to have the painful conversation about his funeral. His body had been ravaged by chemo and and weight loss, his skin hung a little lower on his face, and he was adamant that he not have a funeral at all. He was not a fan of people saying posthumous things about what an amazing man he was when most of the things he did in life were not that amazing (his words, not mine.) At that point, all of us rolled our eyes at him, and as gallows humor is required when you are looking death in the eye, one of us responded, "No offense dad, but your funeral isn't for you. So suck it up."

Which leads me to a video about why love is important in dark times. Brace yourselves, Jesse Parent is about about to talk about farting. If you trust my judgement in any way, I urge you to withhold judgement till at least 1:40. Because this is beautiful.

But when ESPN's Josina Anderson had the opportunity to talk about Michael Sam's football skills she decided to focus on, well, his shower habits (to put it nicely). That's why Cyd Zeigler felt it was time to make this video and start the conversation.

headline: If You Don't Let Your Partner Do This In The Bedroom, You Might As Well Break Up With Them Now
lede:
After my dad was diagnosed with Pancreatic cancer, we had to have the painful conversation about his funeral. His body had been ravaged by chemo and and weight loss, his skin hung a little lower on his face, and he was adamant that he not have a funeral at all. He was not a fan of people saying posthumous things about what an amazing man he was when most of the things he did in life were not that amazing (his words, not mine.) At that point, all of us rolled our eyes at him, and as gallows humor is required when you are looking death in the eye, one of us responded, "No offense dad, but your funeral isn't for you. So suck it up."

Which leads me to a video about why love is important in dark times. Brace yourselves, Jesse Parent is about about to talk about farting. If you trust my judgement in any way, I urge you to withhold judgement till at least 1:40. Because this is beautiful.

headline: The Next Time Some Misguided Soul Says She Was 'Asking For It', Instead Of Getting Mad, Say This
lede:
In a perfect world, a victim of sexual violence would always be met with empathy. Of course, the world is not perfect, and instead victims are often met with skepticism. People will question the validity of their victimization based on the nature of the victim rather than the nature of the perpetrator or the crime.

This doesn't make sense, as Laci Greene demonstrates at 1:05, because we don't apply this sort of logic to any other crimes. But she really brings it home at 1:50 when she goes over the five biggest problems with assigning blame to the victim instead of the perpetrator.

Oh, and next time you're tempted to say something like "what was she wearing?" instead say what Laci says at 4:07.

headline: What Happens When You Take College Kids And Pay Them To Pretend To Be Prisoners And Guards?
lede:

headline: One Mother's Story Of Gun Violence
lede: Kate Ranta's ex-husband was released from a restraining order and immediately went out and purchased a gun. Then he came to her apartment where her father and her 4-year-old son were living with her. Hear her story. Then tell me why you think universal background checks, regardless of private or public sale shouldn't be implemented. It's not a big ask. Her husband would have had a far more expensive time trying to buy a gun. There's a million more Kates in the world, and each one of them has a similar and unnacceptable story to tell.

headline: It's A Parent's Worst Nightmare. And A Kid's. Is Your Family Ready?
lede:
You've probably thought about what your family would do if a hurricane, earthquake, or proletariat uprising disrupted your life. Maybe you imagined yourself huddled with your family in the bathtub, waiting for storm winds to calm. Or helping your kids shove clothes into a duffel bag as the Emergency Broadcast System warned you that This Is Not A Test. Or saving your babies from zombies with only your guts and a tire iron.

But what if your family isn't holed up in the bomb shelter together? Save the Children estimates that, in the United States, 68 million children are separated from their parents, in school or day care, every work day. Maybe it's time to stop the day dream, get with your kids, and make a plan for how you'd get back together.

This is none other than SupaMan, a resident of Montana and member of the Crow Nation — otherwise known as Apsáalooke in the Siouan language. He's a rapper who blends his culture's music with hip-hop. He's got such skills that MTV even featured him.

But he doesn't just sing for First Nations people — he sings for everyone keeping up with "the struggle."

lede: Oh, that good old COLA (Cost Of Living Adjustment). What does it do to the money you make? lede:

Imagine what residents of quiet upstate New York felt when they learned there was one of these rooms sitting quietly on the outskirts of their busy local airport. And then imagine how the military folks involved in this strange stuff reacted when they found protesters outside their gates.

headline: She Crunches Data And She Talks To Jesus, And She's Got A Message
lede:
This interview with Katharine Hayhoe is fascinating and inspiring, no matter your faith. But since there are 80 million evangelical Christians in America, it's especially cool to hear from this person who can crunch the climate-change numbers and be in touch with Jesus.

headline: Is The Princess Culture Something We Can Change?
lede:
Professor Setsu Shigematsu, who is a professor in the Media and Cultural Studies Department of University of California, Riverside, found her efforts at limiting her daughter's exposure to princess culture ineffective. When she refused to buy princess dolls for her then-three-year-old, they only became more desirable. Rather than trying to enforce an impossible ban, she decided to write her own princess story.

That one story has grown into a whole series about princesses who get out there and solve problems, rather than waiting for a guy to save them. I think we can all agree that Prince Charming and his white horse haven't done much for us lately. Time to give the Guardian Princess Alliance a chance?

headline: You Know Those Save The Earth Videos That Make You Feel Like All Is Lost? This Isn't One Of Those.
lede:
Most stuff about the environment makes you seem so small, so insignificant, that you feel powerless to make any kind of tangible change. You say to yourself, "What the hell can I do, I'm just one person." And then you give up, put cotton in your ears, and go back to trying not to think about our place in this world and what we leave behind for our kids, because the alternative is to feel like you just don't have any way to make the situation better, to reverse a millenia of abuse of our systems. headline: The History Of Christopher Columbus, Except This Time With The Actual Facts
lede:
People often get sensitive when you attack their favorite traditions. Columbus Day became a National holiday 77 years ago, after the Knights of Columbus campaigned in NYC to make it happen. It's the only US federal holiday named after a non-American. It's also the only US federal holiday named after a sex slave trader. (Seriously, look it up.)

John Oliver wants to know why Columbus Day is still a thing. So do I. Because of these obvious and glaring facts. And a bunch more. So watch this hilarious video on the subject.
share_text: This Columbus Day let's celebrate by remembering what a murdering psychopath that guy was.

headline: This Mom Was Tired Of Princesses. So She Did Something About It.
lede:
Professor Setsu Shigematsu, who is a professor in the Media and Cultural Studies Department of University of California, Riverside, found her efforts at limiting her daughter's exposure to princess culture ineffective. When she refused to buy princess dolls for her then-three-year-old, they only became more desirable. Rather than trying to enforce an impossible ban, she decided to write her own princess story.

That one story has grown into a whole series about princesses who get out there and solve problems, rather than waiting for a guy to save them. I think we can all agree that Prince Charming and his white horse haven't done much for us lately. Time to give the Guardian Princess Alliance a chance?

But now all these years later, there's finally this.

lede:
Who knew that a bunch of regular moments showing moms at home could be so gorgeous? And intense.

A lot of us either don’t remember or realize how hard our mothers work until we grow up. But these kids already get it. They work long hours, no breaks, no sick days. They've been doing it since the beginning of time, and getting paid nothing but love.

They say that real work is done when no one is looking. But in this case, we see you Moms.

headline: He’s Got A Few Words For Deadbeat Dads Who Leave Their Families For Selfish Reasons
lede:
My first thoughts after watching this were "Awww, what a touching father-and-son story." Then I thought of the last time I'd seen a story like this and got mad.

It's so rare to see a simple portrait of a young black man loving and proudly caring for his child. It’s something that lots of men of color do daily but is rarely shown in the media.

Imagine if you constantly saw men who look like your father being painted as violent, dangerous, untrustworthy, irresponsible, and even criminal? What if your dad was just a regular cool guy? These are the messages that are often fed to all of our children.

So how do we right this wrong? Start by showing everyone more stories like this.
share_text: What’s the biggest, coolest thing that you could ever get from one person? Let him tell it.

headline: 30 Women Who Have Never Met Each Other Have 1 Very Significant Thing In Common
lede:
I think of motherhood as the most incredible thing I never knew I wanted so much until I had it. Before I was a mom, I didn't understand what it felt like to experience true, unconditional love for another human being. And now that I do, I know it's pretty amazing.

At the same time, motherhood is a journey, not a destination. There are ups and downs, great moments and others we might not want to dwell on too much. I think the goal is to do the best we can, and sometimes "best" varies by day.

We may each approach parenting differently, but the best thing we can do for each other is be supportive and lift each other up, just like these women. Because at the end of the day, moms share a common bond: we're all responsible for raising our children. We've got this.

headline: 30 Women Who Have Never Met Each Other Have 1 Very Significant Thing In Common
lede:
I think of motherhood as the most incredible thing I never knew I wanted so much until I had it. Before I was a mom, I didn't understand what it felt like to experience true, unconditional love for another human being. And now that I do, I know it's pretty amazing.

At the same time, motherhood is a journey, not a destination. There are ups and downs, great moments and others we might not want to dwell on too much. I think the goal is to do the best we can, and sometimes "best" varies by day.

We may each approach parenting differently, but the best thing we can do for each other is be supportive and lift each other up, just like these women. Because at the end of the day, moms share a common bond: we're all responsible for raising our children. We've got this.

headline: So Many Famous Folks Have Given This 30 Year Old Anthem The Music Video It Deserves. Rock. On.
lede:
I always liked the Joan Jett song, "Bad Reputation" — it was popular, and it seemed fun and defiant.

It wasn't until I saw this never-ending stream of internet people, movie stars and tv stars singing (and headbanging!) along that I really *listened* to the lyrics. When she sings, "A girl can do what she wants to do and that's what I'm gonna do" it became so clear why they picked this song to send a message to politics.

The message of this song is *exactly* what I wanna tell all the politicians who want to tell women what they can or cannot do for their health and well-being and the safety of their families and children.

I. Don't. Give. A .... well you know the rest. ;)

headline: In 1980, She Made A Statement. In 2014, All These Awesome Famous People Did Too.
lede:
I always liked the song, "Bad Reputation" — you can't deny it, Joan Jett is perhaps the most rock & roll human ever.

But it wasn't until I saw this never-ending stream of internet people, movie stars and TV stars singing (and headbanging!) along that I really *listened* to the lyrics. When she sings, "A girl can do what she wants to do and that's what I'm gonna do..." it became so clear why THIS is the song is what the creators of this video chose.

THIS song says *exactly* what I want to say to uninformed and impolite politicians who think they can tell me what to do.

I. Don't. Give. A .... well you know the rest. ;)

headline: Most People Don't Care. Those That Do, Feel Hopeless. This Video Is For Both Of You.
lede:
Most stuff about the environment makes you seem so small, so insignificant, that you feel powerless to make any kind of tangible change. You say to yourself, "What the hell can I do, I'm just one person." And then you give up, put cotton in your ears, and go back to trying not to think about our place in this world and what we leave behind for our kids, because the alternative is to feel like you just don't have any way to make the situation better, to reverse a millenia of abuse of our systems. You feel like you can't put the cork back in on a bottle we already shook too hard. And so you focus on things you can impact instead.

But you know what I learned in my 2 years of curating about getting people to help change things? When they saw success, even small success on a local level, they felt like there was hope. There was a chance to slowly reverse the damage we have wrought. And that's where this video comes in. It's a pretty simple ask. The only thing I'll ask you to do right now is watch it.

headline: Got 7 Minutes To Be Wildly Inspired? Because This Is Some Seriously Good Stuff.
lede:
Most stuff about the environment makes you seem so small, so insignificant, that you feel powerless to make any kind of tangible change. You say to yourself, "What the hell can I do, I'm just one person." And then you give up, put cotton in your ears, and go back to trying not to think about our place in this world and what we leave behind for our kids, because the alternative is to feel like you just don't have any way to make the situation better, to reverse a millenia of abuse of our systems. You feel like you can't put the cork back in on a bottle we already shook too hard. And so you focus on things you can impact instead.

But you know what I learned in my 2 years of curating about getting people to help change things? When they saw success, even small success on a local level, they felt like there was hope. There was a chance to slowly reverse the damage we have wrought. And that's where this video comes in. It's a pretty simple ask. The only thing I'll ask you to do right now is watch it.
share_text: Cynics, beware.

lede:
Wow. Human rights lawyer Bryan Stevenson gives a stunning talk about injustice in our criminal system. It's a heavy topic, and there's no way to dress it up as uplifting, but at least Stevenson's charisma and engaging stories make it incredibly mesmerizing.

He starts off slow with stories of his grandmother, but by 6 minutes in he's dropping facts about our prisons that many people would much rather ignore. And it just gets better and better — don't miss the hilarious story at 17:35 about the time he asked a judge to try his client as a rich white dude. And my favorite quote of the whole talk comes at 20:35: "The moral arc of the universe is long, but it bends towards justice." Chills, people, CHILLS!

headline: The U.S. Is The Only Country In The World That Does This To 13-Year-Olds. Hint: It's Not Good.
lede:
Wow. Human rights lawyer Bryan Stevenson gives a stunning talk about injustice in our criminal system. It's a heavy topic, and there's no way to dress it up as uplifting, but at least Stevenson's charisma and engaging stories make it incredibly mesmerizing.

He starts off slow with stories of his grandmother, but by 6 minutes in he's dropping facts about our prisons that many people would much rather ignore. And it just gets better and better — don't miss the hilarious story at 17:35 about the time he asked a judge to try his client as a rich white dude. And my favorite quote of the whole talk comes at 20:35: "The moral arc of the universe is long, but it bends towards justice." Chills, people, CHILLS!

headline: A Famous Actress Posed Topless For A Photo Shoot — On 1 Condition. You'll Want To Hear Her Reason.
lede:
In 2004, when Keira Knightley starred in King Arthur, one of the movie's promotional posters showed Keira aiming a bow and arrow at the viewer. The poster was also massively Photoshopped to make her breasts appear at least twice as large.

10 years later, in November 2014, Keira Knightley appeared topless in a photo shoot with Interview Magazine — on the condition that the photographers not digitally edit her breasts or her stomach at all.

Now she's speaking out about the harm that photo manipulation can cause. We can all learn something from her two cents.
share_text: One thing to know about Keira Knightley: She pulls no punches.

headline: The Truth About The Ferguson Case That Most People Won't Acknowledge
lede:
Some things I have learned:

Pro Publica recently did an in-depth analysis and found that black kids between the ages of 15-19 are 21 times more likely to be shot and killed by cops than white kids of the same age. That's an insane statistic. That's per capita, not actual numbers. If you are a black teenage boy, you have a 21x higher risk of being shot by police.

Also, in 2010, Federal prosecutors took 162,000 cases to a grand jury. You know how many DIDN'T go to trial? 6.

Also, Mike Brown's family will never get a state criminal trial to get justice for their son. And the testimony that denied them that right technically doesn't make any sense. Seriously, go read it.

headline: The Truth About The Ferguson Case That Most People Won't Acknowledge
lede:
Some things I have learned:

Pro Publica recently did an in-depth analysis and found that black kids between the ages of 15-19 are 21 times more likely to be shot and killed by cops than white kids of the same age. That's an insane statistic. That's per capita, not actual numbers. If you are a black teenage boy, you have a 21x higher risk of being shot by police.

Also, in 2010, Federal prosecutors took 162,000 cases to a grand jury. You know how many DIDN'T go to trial? 6.

Also, Mike Brown's family will never get a state criminal trial to get justice for their son. And the testimony that denied them that right technically doesn't make any sense. Seriously, go read it.

headline: While The Rest Of The World Wasn't Looking, Mongolia Managed To Achieve Something Kind Of Amazing
lede:
The Overseas Development Institute has released a new report on Mongolia that's amazing. Even though up to 40% of its population is nomadic, the country has found a way to achieve something wealthier nations can only envy: 98% of its girls and 93% of its boys are now getting a secondary education.

Mongolians value the education of their kids above almost everything else, and now their government — flush with money from a mining boom and improved taxation — has taken up the challenge of paying for it. With a completely overhauled modern education policy that's more responsive to families' needs, and with the support of external financing partners, they're actually getting it done.

share_text: Over 150 million people have seen her film, but few English-speakers could understand it. Until now.

lede:
I was driving through the South with my family recently, and we happened through the town of Tuskegee, Alabama. In my mind, 2 things popped up: The Tuskegee Airmen, and some experiment with syphilis. Wait, what?!

Writer Dale Carnegie has inspired me share a little happy with you. A little history: Dale Carnegie is the father of self help books. He wrote the 1936 business communication self-help book How To Win Friends And Influence People, which was so popular that it remains in print today.

headline: 2 Great Actresses Make A True Detective Spoof That Almost Eases My Pain At The New Season's Casting
lede: I really loved the first season of True Detective. It made me see Matthew McConaughey as a serious actor, and I loved the story. I think it's an unfortunate move, but these two fantastic actresses seem to have heard my frustration and made a parody to cheer me up. Women make awesome detective characters, too.

headline: Tired Of Princesses? So Was This Mom. So She Did Something About It.
lede:
Professor Setsu Shigematsu, who is a professor in the Media and Cultural Studies Department of University of California, Riverside, found her efforts at limiting her daughter's exposure to princess culture ineffective. When she refused to buy princess dolls for her then-three-year-old, they only became more desirable. Rather than trying to enforce an impossible ban, she decided to write her own princess story.

That one story has grown into a whole series about princesses who get out there and solve problems, rather than waiting for a guy to save them. I think we can all agree that Prince Charming and his white horse haven't done much for us lately. Time to give the Guardian Princess Alliance a chance?

headline: You Know Those Save The Earth Videos That Make You Feel Like All Is Lost? This Isn't One Of Those.
lede:
Most stuff about the environment makes you seem so small, so insignificant, that you feel powerless to make any kind of tangible change. You say to yourself, "What the hell can I do, I'm just one person." And then you give up, put cotton in your ears, and go back to trying not to think about our place in this world and what we leave behind for our kids, because the alternative is to feel like you just don't have any way to make the situation better, to reverse a millenia of abuse of our systems. You feel like you can't put the cork back in on a bottle we already shook too hard. And so you focus on things you can impact instead.

But you know what I learned in my 2 years of curating about getting people to help change things? When they saw success, even small success on a local level, they felt like there was hope. There was a chance to slowly reverse the damage we have wrought. And that's where this video comes in. It's a pretty simple ask. The only thing I'll ask you to do right now is watch it.

It's the only US federal holiday named after a non-American. It's also the only US federal holiday named after a sex slave trader. (Seriously, look it up.)

John Oliver wants to know why Columbus Day is still a thing. So do I. Because of these obvious and glaring facts. And a bunch more. So watch this hilarious video on the subject.

headline: This Mom Was Tired Of Princesses. So She Did Something About It.
lede:
Professor Setsu Shigematsu, who is a professor in the Media and Cultural Studies Department of University of California, Riverside, found her efforts at limiting her daughter's exposure to princess culture ineffective. When she refused to buy princess dolls for her then-three-year-old, they only became more desirable. Rather than trying to enforce an impossible ban, she decided to write her own princess story.

That one story has grown into a whole series about princesses who get out there and solve problems, rather than waiting for a guy to save them. I think we can all agree that Prince Charming and his white horse haven't done much for us lately. Time to give the Guardian Princess Alliance a chance?
share_text: This has been a thousand years in the making.

lede: Epidermolysis Bullosa is a disease I had never heard of until today. 30,000 people in the United States today have it. It essentially makes your skin and organs extremely fragile. Children with it have their fingers slowly fused together into mitten shapes. Skin that is cut never heals. Families can spend as much as $14,000 a month on bandaging alone. Athletic and physical activities are out of the question. They are prone to skin cancer. And one of them happens to be friends with Pearl Jam's Eddie Vedder. headline: He’s Got A Few Words For Deadbeat Dads Who Leave Their Families For Selfish Reasons
lede:
Traditionally dads were pressured to pour all of their time into their careers to be “good providers,” all while some of them missed out on being good dads. Now that more folks split work and parenting duties evenly, more dads hang with their kids.

But what does it mean to be a good father? Most people automatically assume money. Some kids are too young to vocalize it, but what always wins is something that most can afford — good ‘ole fashioned time.

(Okay, so stay with me here, because here’s where I get all Hallmarky … but it’s true).

Sometimes just being there for your kid, caring for them, is what truly makes a difference. It can mean pushing them on a tricycle down a crowded city street or making their favorite breakfast, even if everyone else thinks that your cinnamon pancakes with a touch of lime are horrific.

Whether it’s the big moments — first steps or first words, or the everyday ones, it’s great that dads like the man featured in this video, can be there to share them all.

headline: 30 Women Who Have Never Met Each Other Have 1 Very Significant Thing In Common
lede:
I think of motherhood as the most incredible thing I never knew I wanted so much until I had it. Before I was a mom, I didn't understand what it felt like to experience true, unconditional love for another human being. And now that I do, I know it's pretty amazing.

At the same time, motherhood is a journey, not a destination. There are ups and downs, great moments and others we might not want to dwell on too much. I think the goal is to do the best we can, and sometimes "best" varies by day.

We may each approach parenting differently, but the best thing we can do for each other is be supportive and lift each other up, just like these women. Because at the end of the day, moms share a common bond: we're all responsible for raising our children. We've got this.

headline: These Famous Folks Have A Not-So-Hidden Message Behind What They're Singing
lede:
I always liked the Joan Jett song, "Bad Reputation" — it was popular, and it seemed fun and defiant.

It wasn't until I saw this never-ending stream of internet people, movie stars and tv stars singing (and headbanging!) along that I really *listened* to the lyrics. When she sings, "A girl can do what she wants to do and that's what I'm gonna do" it became so clear why they picked this song to send a message to politics.

The message of this song is *exactly* what I wanna tell all the politicians who want to tell women what they can or cannot do for their health and well-being and the safety of their families and children.

I. Don't. Give. A .... well you know the rest. ;)

headline: Got 7 Minutes To Be Wildly Inspired? Because This Is Some Seriously Good Stuff.
lede:
Most stuff about the environment makes you seem so small, so insignificant, that you feel powerless to make any kind of tangible change. You say to yourself, "What the hell can I do, I'm just one person." And then you give up, put cotton in your ears, and go back to trying not to think about our place in this world and what we leave behind for our kids, because the alternative is to feel like you just don't have any way to make the situation better, to reverse a millenia of abuse of our systems. You feel like you can't put the cork back in on a bottle we already shook too hard. And so you focus on things you can impact instead.

But you know what I learned in my 2 years of curating about getting people to help change things? When they saw success, even small success on a local level, they felt like there was hope. There was a chance to slowly reverse the damage we have wrought. And that's where this video comes in. It's a pretty simple ask. The only thing I'll ask you to do right now is watch it.

headline: A Famous Actress Posed Topless For A Photo Shoot — On 1 Condition. You'll Want To Hear Her Reason.
lede:
In 2004, when Keira Knightley starred in King Arthur, one of the movie's promotional posters showed Keira aiming a bow and arrow at the viewer. The poster was also massively Photoshopped to make her breasts appear at least twice as large.

10 years later, in November 2014, Keira Knightley appeared topless in a photo shoot with Interview Magazine — on the condition that the photographers not digitally edit her breasts or her stomach at all.

Now she's speaking out about the harm that photo manipulation can cause. We can all learn something from her two cents.
share_text: Keira Knightley did something bold — all for a good cause.

headline: Why Do Sexual Assault Survivors Feel Shame? A Cartoon Sums It Up. By The 4th Panel, I'm Taken Aback.
lede:
Trigger warning: Discussion of rape, sexual assault, abuse.

Almost every survivor of sexual assault or abuse will at one point think, "It was my fault." What many of us don't know is WHY survivors feel shame and guilt or why others around them might blame them instead of the perpetrator. The following cartoon breaks down the reasons why.

So, to all the survivors out there who are blaming themselves for what happened, here's the psychology behind why you might feel so guilty. I'm crossing my fingers that at least a couple of you will read this and finally feel some solace.

And for anyone who has ever asked, "Why didn't she run away?" or "Why didn't he scream?" This one's for you, too.
